articles.title: How Will AI Affect Open Source Development?
articles.body:
How Will AI Affect Open Source Development? (linuxfoundation.org) 29
			
		 	
				This week the Linux Foundation's Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) announced it would broaden its AI security resources, including a new guide to finding and fixing vulnerabilities using AI, "from preparing and sandboxing AI to validating, fixing, and preventing issues."  The guide "stresses that AI-generated patches should never be trusted without automated tests and human review. An online course (LFD126) is planned for the coming months."
OpenSSF also released the State of AI Impact on Software Security and Cybersecurity 2026 report (supported by OpenSSF, ActiveState and the Linux Foundation AI & Data Foundation). And it turns out the 2026 report "found a growing gap between the pace of AI-driven software development and organizations' ability to secure the code being produced."
 58% of surveyed teams ship code faster than security reviews can keep up, while 60% say AI coding assistants have increased the number of external packages in their codebases. This data underscores the importance of trusted, reliable guidance as AI deployment continues to grow. 
Meanwhile the Linux Foundation announced at this week's Web Summit that it was releasing a new study on "how commercial open source companies generate revenue, convert users into customers and build their businesses," emphasizing the question's new relevance in the age of AI.  "AI now writes code almost for free, and that raises a hard question for the whole software industry: if code costs next to nothing, where does the value of software lie?"
Commercial open source [COSS] companies have been answering that question for more than 30 years. They have built large businesses on code they give away, which makes them a good guide to how software will make money in the age of AI...  Seventy-two percent of respondents report a net positive impact from AI, against 8% negative. So far, the gains show up mostly inside companies. Internal productivity is the most cited benefit (73%), ahead of market expansion (46%) and new monetization opportunities (39%). AI roles are the only hiring category growing on net.
COSS strategy is mostly unchanged by AI. But when companies do adapt, they are nearly twice as likely to open more of their core product rather than become more closed.  When asked what sets them apart, 57% of companies name brand recognition and trust, well ahead of enterprise features, integrations and community size. They turn that trust into revenue through support and services (63%), managed cloud (49%) and open core (43%). Most combine these: 65% run two or more revenue models. 
Companies stack models as they grow, rather than switching between them: managed cloud rises from 35% of companies below $5 million ARR to 66% above $20 million. Venture-backed companies lean toward open core (53% vs. 38% for others). 
The report draws on a survey of 225 commercial open source founders and enterprise leaders (published by Linux Foundation Research in partnership with Serena,  and with sponsorship from AWS, Red Hat, Futurewei and the  Cloud Native Computing Foundation.  And when it comes to open source, "over half of founders point to brand recognition and community trust as their greatest asset," said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.  So
"The findings from this year's report prove that AI isn't a threat to commercial open source software — it's an accelerating tailwind.  With 72% of companies viewing AI as a net positive primarily driving internal productivity, the ecosystem is leaning further into collaboration." 
The Linux Foundation's announcement includes an interesting perspective from Matthieu Lavergne, partner at the venture capital company Serena.  "Open source won the developer. Next, it will win the agent. The 225 founders we surveyed mostly see AI as a productivity gain today, but that's only the start: agents are set to become open source's largest users, and they choose what is open, proven and trusted. The founders who build and price for these new users will define the infrastructure of the AI era."

articles.title: Did Alice Huang's Megaspeed Bypass America's Controls on Exporting Nvidia Chip to China?
articles.body:
Did Alice Huang's Megaspeed Bypass America's Controls on Exporting Nvidia Chip to China? (cnn.com) 34
			
		 	
				In three years "Megaspeed International" went from from inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary "to one of Asia's biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US," reports CNN.
"It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks," trade data investigator William George told CNN. 
As Nvidia's Jensen Huang had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, "Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia," CNN writes, noting scrutiny of the company from the Singapore government and US officials "concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers..."
In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia's most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China's tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them.  US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those...   [T]rade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia... Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year... 
Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company's server purchases and their final destinations.   In a statement, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence that Huang had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information "to downplay her role" at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing.
The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws. A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia.  
CNN reminds readers that Jensen Huang accompanied US President Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, and also lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports.  "The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue."
"However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well," they add.  And the Taiwanese government is even seeking to criminalize unauthorized exports of advanced AI chips to China, "as prosecutors there charged nine people in a scheme to sneak Nvidia chips into China through Japan, Indonesia and Hong Kong."

articles.title: Show HN: Turbo-Browser-MCP – Batch forms, DOM deltas and submit guards for MCP
articles.body:
turbo-browser-mcp is a Playwright-based Model Context Protocol (MCP) server built to cut LLM token waste and multi-turn latency in browser automation. It consolidates 25-33 fine-grained browser primitives into 10 batched tools featuring delta DOM snapshots, single-turn React/Shadow DOM/iframe form prefill, direct disk file uploads (no Base64 in context), parallel tab sessions, network blocking presets, and a default human-in-the-loop Submit guard.
All figures below come from benchmarks/benchmark.mjs (npm run benchmark) running headless Chromium locally with exact OpenAI o200k_base tokenization (tiktoken 0.14.0):
Note on latency vs LLM inference turns: Eliminating 10 round-trips on a 10-field form saves both 7x in browser execution (574 ms -> 82 ms) and 10 separate LLM inference round-trips (2-5s per turn in agent loops) plus ~71,800 replayed history tokens.
Standard MCP servers charge an LLM round-trip for every snapshot, field fill, <select> choice, upload, and verification check. Each turn re-sends the growing conversation history back into the model.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Agent as LLM Agent
    participant Std as Standard MCP (Playwright / DevTools)
    participant Turbo as turbo-browser-mcp
    Note over Agent,Std: Standard MCP (12+ LLM turns, full ARIA tree + history replay each step)
    Agent->>Std: 1. snapshot() -> full ARIA (~3,568 tok)
    loop Repeats 10+ times across fields, selects, checkboxes, upload
        Agent->>Std: fill / select_option / click
        Std-->>Agent: full ARIA or confirmation re-added to history
    end
    Agent->>Std: 12. upload inline or click chooser
    Note over Agent,Turbo: turbo-browser-mcp (2 LLM turns total, delta & inline snapshot)
    Agent->>Turbo: 1. inspect_compact(mode: "forms") -> compact refs (1,135 tok)
    Agent->>Turbo: 2. smart_fill_form(fields: [...10 fields + disk PDF...], returnSnapshot: true)
    Turbo-->>Agent: Filled 10 fields + guarded before Submit + inline snapshot (811 tok)
    - 4 connection modes (--mode auto|cdp|persistent|launch):
  - auto (default): probes --cdp http://127.0.0.1:9222 first so agents can reuse an existing signed-in browser session, then falls back to launching Chromium.
  - cdp: attach directly to a running Chromium/Chrome/Edge remote debugging port.
  - persistent: launch with a reusable --user-data-dir profile across runs.
  - launch: start a clean browser session (--headless by default, or --headed).
- Auto binary discovery (src/playwright-loader.mjs): checks playwright-core cache revisions across Windows, macOS, and Linux, system installs of Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Brave, and Chromium, or an explicit --executable <path>.
- Per-tab isolation (tabs_batch): open tabs inside named isolatedContext sandboxes with separate cookies and storage, batch-open up to 10 concurrent URLs (open_many), activate, reload, go back/forward, resize viewport, and emulate colorScheme, media, reducedMotion, contrast, forcedColors, or custom userAgent.
- Snapshot modes: interactive, forms, article, and all.
- Cross-boundary traversal: flattens main frame DOM, child iframes (includeFrames, frameIdx), and open Shadow DOM. Injects an init script hooking Element.prototype.attachShadow (WeakMap + WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry + window.__tbmGetShadowRoot) to keep post-init closed Shadow roots inspectable and guarded, traverses <slot> assignedNodes({ flatten: true }), and supports Form-Associated Custom Elements.
- Token controls: onlyChanged: true emits only elements added or changed since the prior snapshot; query filters by regex or substring; boxes: true adds [box=x,y,w,h] only when needed; maxChars caps payload size; savePath writes full output to disk.
Prefills an entire form in one MCP call while flushing microtasks and macrotasks between controlled inputs:
- Standard & framework inputs: text, email, password, number, date, textarea, <input type="range">, checkboxes, radio groups (check, not, overwrite). Triggers React-controlled state updates via native property setters and synthetic events.
- Selects & custom widgets: <select> and <select multiple> (option / values), ARIA comboboxes, ARIA switches, contenteditable rich editors, and Gmail compose dialogs (gmail: { to, subject, body }).
- Frame & wildcard targeting: target specific iframes via frameIdx, or set all: true to populate matching controls across frames.
- Direct disk uploads: pass file or files paths directly to Playwright setInputFiles without loading binary files or Base64 strings into LLM context.
- Atomic verification: pass returnSnapshot: true to inspect the updated form state in the same tool response.
- act_fast actions: click, dblclick, hover, focus, clear, fill, type (slowly, delayMs, submit), select, check, uncheck, drag, drop (file, files, or custom MIME dropData), press (key + modifiers: Alt, Control, ControlOrMeta, Meta, Shift), scroll (dx, dy), wait (ms, state, loadState, text, textGone, url), and upload.
- Targeting options: compact [eN] ref, CSS selector, visible text, label, or viewport (x, y) coordinates, with button (left, right, middle) and frameIdx.
- batch_actions: runs an ordered list of DOM actions and nested smart_fill_form steps in one MCP call, stopping safely if blocked by the Submit guard or optionally continuing on step errors (continueOnError).
- extract_clean_text: extracts readable plain text or compact Markdown (format: "text" | "markdown") from main/article containers and iframes, stripped of script and style noise.
- evaluate_js: runs JS expressions or (el, arg) element functions in any frame (frameIdx) with JSON-serialized results and optional savePath export.
- capture_page: full-page or element-scoped screenshots (png or jpeg with quality, css or device scale, optional returnImage) and PDF generation saved to a confined savePath.
- network_session presets: turbo, no-images, no-media, and clean (unblock all), alongside custom blockResources and blockUrls patterns.
- Session & storage management: read/write/clear browser cookies, localStorage/sessionStorage, and export or reload full Playwright storageState JSON files (saveStorageStatePath, loadStorageStatePath).
- page_diagnostics: defaults to errors-only (level: "errors", statusFilter: "errors") to surface failures cleanly without flooding context, while supporting all, includeStatic, urlFilter, deep request/response inspection (reqId + part), completed downloads, and dialog auto-handling (dialogPolicy: accept/dismiss).
Run the benchmark suite yourself with Chromium and Playwright installed:
npm run benchmark
Environment & methodology: Headless Chromium via playwright-core, counting exact OpenAI o200k_base tokens via Python tiktoken (approx-bpe fallback if tiktoken is unavailable). Cumulative workflow tokens model standard chat-history replay across $N$ sequential turns: $\sum_{i=1}^{N} (N - i + 1) \cdot T_i$, plus a one-shot baseline where the first turn captures context before acting.
Measured against installed MCP JSON schemas on disk (compact parameter schemas without annotations):
v0.5.0 added wait_for_human and the commit-safety parameters for about 160 tokens per turn (v0.4.0: 3,010 compact). To keep that small, expect / submissionKey / allowDuplicate are declared only on batch_actions (a one-step batch works for a single click), and the network guard is switched on by environment variable, so it costs no schema tokens. The label lists for other languages run inside the page and are never sent to the model.
When to keep Chrome DevTools MCP alongside turbo-browser-mcp: chrome-devtools-mcp provides Lighthouse audits, performance trace analysis, CSS computed style panels, and V8 heap snapshots. turbo-browser-mcp focuses on fast multi-step UI automation, forms, and scraping with minimal token overhead.
- Human-in-the-loop Submit Guard (allowSubmit=false by default):
  - smart_fill_form (stopBeforeSubmit: true), act_fast, and batch_actions inspect matching elements, W3C AccName labels (isSafeSubmitter), implicit HTML form Enter submissions, key chords (Shift+Enter, Enter+Shift), HTMLFormElement.prototype.submit/requestSubmit, and same-origin iframe contentWindow/contentDocument proxies.
  - Final actions resembling Submit, Publish, Send, Post, Apply, Confirm, or payment triggers are blocked unless allowSubmit: true is explicitly passed or --allow-submit is enabled at startup.
  - Trade-off: pre-existing closed Shadow roots on already-open CDP tabs (attached before the init script ran) or strict cross-origin sandboxed frames fall back to Playwright frame handles, coordinate actions, and keyboard input.
- Workspace Path Confinement (TURBO_BROWSER_SAVE_ROOT):
  - File outputs (savePath, saveStorageStatePath) and state inputs (loadStorageStatePath) are strictly confined to the current working directory or TURBO_BROWSER_SAVE_ROOT.
  - Lexical checks, lstatSync/readlinkSync symlink verification, and realpathSync validation block .. traversal, UNC network paths, dangling symlinks, cyclic symlinks, and Windows junctions before reading or writing.
Readers who run agents on real portals pointed out three gaps in a label-based guard. v0.5.0 adds an opt-in answer to each. expect, submissionKey and allowDuplicate appear in the batch_actions schema; act_fast accepts the same arguments without advertising them. The network guard is turned on with TURBO_BROWSER_NETWORK_GUARD=true and covers act_fast, batch_actions and smart_fill_form.
- A landed click is not a confirmed submission → expect. After an allowed submit, pass expect: { urlMatches?, textMatches?, selector?, timeoutMs? }. The result carries submitVerified and evidence (the new URL, a text snippet such as a receipt number, or the matched selector). If nothing shows up in time you get submitVerified: false and a reason, so the agent does not report "done" on an empty submission list.
- A re-run is a second entry, not a retry → submissionKey. With submissionKey: "portal:2026-11-15:entry-42", every allowed submit is appended to a JSONL ledger (~/.turbo-browser-mcp/submissions.jsonl, or TURBO_BROWSER_LEDGER, or ledgerPath inside the save root). A later call with the same key is refused with blockedBy: "ledger" unless allowDuplicate: true.
- Labels lie → modal rule + networkGuard. On many Korean portals the last step reads 다음 and the real commit is a 확인 inside a modal that opens afterwards.
  - Affirmative buttons (확인, OK, Yes, Confirm, 確認, 确定, Đồng ý, …) inside dialog / [role=dialog] / [role=alertdialog] / [aria-modal=true] now count as commits (blockedBy: "modal"). Cookie banners (dialog text mentions cookies) and date/time pickers (dialog contains a calendar grid or date input) are excluded; a confirmation that only mentions "privacy" or "consent" is still blocked.
  - When an action makes the page call form.submit() / requestSubmit() or fire a submit event and the guard stops it, the result now says so (submitSuppressed, note) instead of a bare ok: true. The action itself (a select, a check) still counts as done, so batches continue.
  - Common Korean, Japanese, Chinese and Vietnamese submit labels were added (제출, 신청, 등록, 결제, 送信, 確定, 提交, Hoàn tất, …), and 다음, 次へ, 下一步 are treated like Next.
  - TURBO_BROWSER_NETWORK_GUARD=true is the safety net that does not depend on labels: while submitting is not allowed, non-GET navigations and same-site fetch/XHR POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE are stopped and reported (blockedBy: "network", networkBlocked[]). Blocked navigations get a 204 so the page and the half-filled form stay put. Let harmless endpoints through with TURBO_BROWSER_NETWORK_GUARD_ALLOW="/autosave$,/analytics". Per call, the undeclared arguments networkGuard, networkGuardAllow and networkGuardSettleMs override the env values. It is off by default because multi-step wizards often POST on every "Next".
  - Every blocked result now says which mechanism stopped it: blockedBy is label, modal, network or ledger.
Limits:
- The network guard watches the action plus networkGuardSettleMs (250 ms) afterwards, so a commit fired later by a timer is not caught. WebSocket messages, requests made by a service worker, and cross-site fetch POSTs are not inspected (cross-site navigations are). Patterns in TURBO_BROWSER_NETWORK_GUARD_ALLOW are split on commas, so a pattern cannot contain one.
- The ledger is written only when the call returns. If the call throws after the page already sent the submission (for example a navigation timeout), nothing is recorded; check the site before re-running.
- expect.selector that is not a valid selector never matches, so the call reports submitVerified: false after the timeout.
Some sites fail their bot check whenever the browser is remote-controlled, so a person has to open the same profile in a normal browser first. turbo-browser-mcp does not try to hide automation: no stealth plugins, no fingerprint or navigator.webdriver patching, no CAPTCHA solving. It supports two hand-off flows instead.
- Before the session: turbo-browser-mcp --open-profile --url https://site.example/login opens plain Chrome (no debugging port, no automation flags) on the dedicated profile ~/.turbo-browser-mcp/chrome-profile (or --user-data-dir). The human logs in or passes the check and closes the window. Then start the server with --user-data-dir <same path> or --launch-chrome, and the agent reuses those cookies. This works for sites that check at login; a site that re-checks on every request will still see an automated browser.
- During the session: the agent calls wait_for_human with a message and a condition (urlMatches, selector, textMatches or textGone). The tool brings the tab to the front and polls until the condition holds, then the agent continues in the same tab with the same cookies. Keep timeoutMs below your MCP client's request timeout and call it again to keep waiting.
{
  "name": "wait_for_human",
  "arguments": {
    "message": "Please sign in and finish the security check, then leave the tab open.",
    "selector": "#account-menu",
    "timeoutMs": 120000
  }
}{
  "name": "batch_actions",
  "arguments": {
    "steps": [
      { "action": "smart_fill_form", "fields": [{ "selector": "#name", "value": "홍길동" }] },
      { "action": "click", "text": "다음" },
      { "action": "click", "text": "확인" }
    ],
    "allowSubmit": true,
    "expect": { "textMatches": "접수번호\\s*R-\\d+", "timeoutMs": 8000 },
    "submissionKey": "photo-contest:2026-11-15:entry-1"
  }
}{
  "name": "smart_fill_form",
  "arguments": {
    "fields": [
      { "selector": "#full_name", "value": "Alex Nguyen" },
      { "selector": "#email", "value": "alex@example.com" },
      { "selector": "#country", "option": "United States" },
      { "selector": "#skills", "values": ["TypeScript", "Playwright"] },
      { "selector": "#agree_terms", "check": true },
      { "selector": "#resume_pdf", "file": "./assets/resume.pdf" }
    ],
    "stopBeforeSubmit": true,
    "returnSnapshot": true
  }
}{
  "name": "inspect_compact",
  "arguments": {
    "mode": "interactive",
    "onlyChanged": true,
    "maxChars": 3000
  }
}{
  "name": "tabs_batch",
  "arguments": {
    "operations": [
      { "action": "open", "url": "https://example.com/app", "isolatedContext": "acct-a" },
      { "action": "open_many", "urls": ["https://example.com/docs", "https://example.com/pricing"], "concurrency": 4 }
    ]
  }
}git clone https://github.com/Tthanh2k6/turbo-browser-mcp.git
cd turbo-browser-mcp
npm install
npm run doctor
If you need Playwright's bundled Chromium (or have no system Chrome/Edge/Brave installed):
npx playwright-core install chromium
Using local clone:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "turbo-browser": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/absolute/path/to/turbo-browser-mcp/src/index.mjs"],
      "env": {
        "TURBO_BROWSER_SAVE_ROOT": "/absolute/path/to/allowed/workspace"
      }
    }
  }
}
Using npx / binary entrypoint:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "turbo-browser": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "turbo-browser-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
In Chrome 136+/144+, enabling chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging on the default User Data directory exposes a WebSocket in DevToolsActivePort that displays an "Allow remote debugging?" prompt whenever a new WebSocket client connects. turbo-browser-mcp provides two built-in solutions so overnight AFK multi-agent runs never hang on a prompt:
- Automatic CDP Keep-Alive Bridge Daemon (npm run bridge / --bridge, enabled automatically on DevToolsActivePort):
  - Spawns a detached background multiplexer (src/cdp-bridge.mjs on http://127.0.0.1:9224) that holds one persistent upstream WebSocket to Chrome open indefinitely and intercepts Browser.close so downstream scripts never terminate your browser.
  - You click Allow once when starting your session; afterwards, any number of MCP servers, CLI scripts, or subagents can connect and disconnect all night with 0 additional prompts.
- Zero-Prompt Dedicated Profile Launcher (npm run launch-chrome / --launch-chrome):
  - Launches Chrome with --remote-debugging-port=9222 and a dedicated --user-data-dir (~/.turbo-browser-mcp/chrome-profile), where Chrome exposes standard HTTP/WS CDP with 0 confirmation dialogs even on the very first connection.
npm test            # 424 passing tests across 87 suites (27 test files under test/*.test.mjs)
npm run doctor      # Environment check for Node, Playwright, Chromium, and CDP
npm run bridge      # Start/verify persistent CDP Keep-Alive Bridge daemon
npm run benchmark   # Local Chromium speed & exact o200k_base token benchmark
npm run benchmark:e2e  # End-to-end wizard task + commit-safety cases (see benchmarks/E2E_COMPARISON.md)
Tested automatically on GitHub Actions (ubuntu-latest) across Node 20 and Node 22.

articles.title: Book list for streetfighting computer scientists
articles.body:
Book list for streetfighting computer scientists
2025 edition. this is very different from most "best books for programmers" lists you'll see, with Code Complete and Clean Code and Wistful Wanking for Practical Wankers and Design Slatterns and titles like that. you'll figure all that out as you go along. these are books to read so that you can cut motherfuckers with knives. do you need to read all of these? only if you want to know the things inside, i guess.
Introductory streetfighting
- Stepanov, From Mathematics to Generic Programming and The Elements of Programming
- Gustedt, Modern C
- Hanson, C Interfaces and Implementations
- Stroustrup, The C++ Programming Language
- Josuttis, C++ Move Semantics, because a language feature requiring 200 pages of explication is worth studying? no, because this book justifies Rust better than any text on that language.
- Klabnik, Nichols, and Krycho, The Rust Programming Language
need you write in C or C++? not generally. but they are a lingua franca, implemented on most hardware you'll meet, and serve as the native API expression of all operating system that matter. rust is a pretty good language to write and read, and much less to talk about all the fucking time, so cut that shit out.
Brawling combat
- Dijkstra, A Discipline of Programming. the most beautiful book, page-for-page, in all of computer science.
- Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, especially volumes 1 and 4B, third edition
- Warren, Hacker's Delight. make sure you get the second edition
- Stevens and Rago, Advanced Programming in the UNIX Environment, get at least the second and preferably the third edition
- Stevens, UNIX Network Programming, second edition
- Abelson + Sussman, Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, best cover on a CS textbook hands down, second edition
- Varghese, Networking Algorithmics
- McKusick, The Design and Implementation of the FreeBSD Operating System
- Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface
- Garcia + Widjaja, Communications Networks. do you even ARQ, bro?
- Kleinrock, Queueing Systems, especially volume 1. this is why they made you take prob/stats.
- Hennessy + Paterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. the older editions don't lock material away from you online, but are...older.
- Kennedy, Optimizing Compilers for Modern Architectures. if you want to actually implement compilers make sure you get Muchnik's Advanced Compiler Design and Implmentation as well
- CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms
- Samet, Metric and Multidimensional Data Structures
- McKenney, Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It? despite its preposterous title, this book is excellent, and covers things you won't find anywhere else. If Naming Books is so Hard for You, Why Didn't You Ask For Help?
- Crochemere et al, Algorithms on Strings. just as french as it sounds, a true force de frappe
- Culler et al, Parallel Computer Architecture
- Ward + Halstead, Computation Structures
- Shriver + Smith, The Anatomy of a High-Performance Microprocessor
- Vazirani, Approximation Algorithms
- Raghaven + Motwani, Randomized Algorithms
- Garey and Johnson, Computers and Intractability. it's always embarrassing to realize you've promised a solution to an np-complete problem.
- Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation. but not as embarrassing as realizing you've promised a solution to an undecidable problem. also, the pumping lemma!
- Galub + Van Loan, Matrix Computations. this is pretty much a straight mathematics textbook, but roaming multiethnic gangs of matrices make up many streetfights.
For the advanced streetfighter
- Ahora + Barak, Computational Complexity
- Pierce, Types and Programming Languages
- Okasaki, Purely Functional Data Structures
- Van Roy + Hardidi, Concepts, Techniques, and Models of Computer Programming
- Barendregt, The Lambda Calculus. it is true that the λ-cube is rarely useful within the tight confines of a knifefight. after a long day of bandanas and leather gloves and switchblades, even the brawler must eventually go home to family and fire and food and F systems. in a pinch, its bedazzling yellow cover can blind opponents.
speaking of math, you might want to take a look at Axler's Linear Algebra Done Right and Knuth's Concrete Mathematics. you'll want to know your combinatorics, your prob/stats, and your linear algebra cold. calculus through diffeqs is necessary to know, but i'm a pretty hardcore nerd and yet don't find myself integrating things all that often.
now go forth and fight in the streets. i list no machine learning because i dislike machine learning. there are no quantum books because quantum is not yet useful for streetfighting (we all look forward to this situation changing). i list no SIMT/accelerator books because they're all shite. i list no infosec because infosec is a subfield of QA, fight me. there are no links because i'm a lazy, lazy man.
i've heard good things about Tim Roughgarden's algorithms books, and have them on my shelves to read soon, but cannot yet speak to them. likewise Beej's book on networking, though that looks kinda lightweight. neither he nor Stevens goes into modern fast networking using things like XDP and Io_uring.
you should of course also read Hacking the Planet with Notcurses, buying copies for your team and family.

articles.title: GTA 6's Upcoming Launch Celebrated by Wendy's, YouTube, the City of Miami, and 20% of America's Workforce
articles.body:
GTA 6's Upcoming Launch Celebrated by Wendy's, YouTube, the City of Miami, and 20% of America's Workforce (gamingbible.com) 8
			
		 	
				Fast food restaurant Wendy's drew an image of their redheaded mascot in the style of GTA, posting it on social media with the message "Our ride-or-dies are gonna love what we have in the works," and the date 11/19/26.
That's how widespread the hype has become for Thursday's release of Grand Theft Auto VI.
The BBC reports that fictional brands from the game are now actually appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game's "Vice City" setting. And  GamingBible.com reports Rockstar Games has announced Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival, "a real-life music festival to be held in Miami, Florida...  on November 21, 2026.  Featuring two stages, the festival will be headlined by some incredible artists that, to state the obvious, feature on the game's soundtrack...."
YouTube said pre-launch videos about the game have already racked up a whopping 40 billion views (with 900 billion views for videos about all GTA games).  And now YouTube is partnering with Rockstar Games to offer several special features on launch day:
Fans can drop themselves directly into Vice City using the GTAVI: Visit Vice City Shorts Effect. The feature includes multiple iconic backgrounds, making it easy for creators and fans to build their own launch-week videos... 
Listeners can find the official GTAVI soundtrack (featuring Morgan Wallen's "Last Thing You Need") and the complete GTA series anthology playlist directly on the YouTube Music homepage throughout launch week...
Starting November 19 at 12 AM ET, fans worldwide can tune in to youtube.com/youtube for a 24 hour stream packed with live gameplay, creator podcasts, and original content featuring top creators... [On launch day] fans can jump straight into the global broadcast by clicking the custom GTAVI-themed YouTube logo (Yoodle) on the YouTube homepage  
At one one study suggests nearly one in a five U.S. workers plan to skip work on Thursday, writes
the New York Post:
Roughly 18% of workers plan to take Thursday off to park themselves on the couch and wreak havoc across the revamped Vice City, according to data from BambooHR, which analyzed information from 3.4 million US-based employees... Half of the joystick jockeys planning to take off will simply call in sick instead of requesting time off, BambooHR reported.  The hordes of workers playing hooky could cost the US economy $1 billion in lost productivity, International Business News reported.  
Forbes reports the game has $1.18 billion in pre-orders from 12 million buyers, according to market research firm Sensor Tower, puting it ahead of Grand Theft Auto V, which had 7 million pre-orders. 
The BBC points out that "Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history.  This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it. 
But that's a problem for other games, reports GamingBible.com:
With most current-gen consoles having somewhere between 512 GB and 1 TB of free storage before expansion upgrades, it means if you're a gamer with lots of games installed, you're going to have to make some sacrifices and delete any older games you're not currently playing.  As reported by Push Square, it seems that Electronic Arts is also getting the message, as it allegedly is showing messages inside games asking players not to uninstall in anticipation of the GTA VI launch. 
GamingBible.com notes one final concern for hardcore gamers.  "Rockstar Games recently confirmed the game targets 30fps, even on high-end consoles like the PlayStation Pro.  While it probably won't affect the game's total sales, many gamers are appalled."

articles.title: Bitcoin Plummets 24% in 46 Days as Crypto Falls on Rising Inflation
articles.body:
Bitcoin Plummets 24% in 46 Days as Crypto Falls on Rising Inflation (fastcompany.com) 50
			
		 	
				October 3:  $84,680
Today:  $64,108
Bitcoin dropped 24.2% in 46 days.  And it "fell more than 4% on Friday to $68,500," reports Fortune, "wiping out gains built over the past three months and casting doubt on whether its bear market was ever really over."
The asset also faces weaker investor appetite, according to crypto analytics provider CryptoQuant. The firm's demand indicator recorded its weakest reading since December 2023, while Bitcoin exchange-traded funds became net sellers again.   The recent downturn has also extended to other parts of the crypto market. That includes Tether's USDT, the largest cryptocurrency pegged to the U.S. dollar, whose total value shrank by $7.7 billion over the past two months, according to CryptoQuant, a sign that less cash is available in crypto markets.
This time around, inflation has been the main culprit. Tuesday's Consumer Price Index report showed prices rose 0.4% in October, more than economists expected. Even stripping out food and energy, inflation ran hotter than forecast. Traders now overwhelmingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point in December, with some betting on an even bigger increase.   "Because these are non-yielding assets, and we expect inflation to rise... people are chucking stuff like gold and Bitcoin to find... government bonds that are going up, providing you [with] income," Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at financial technology company IG Group, told Fortune...
Heavy borrowing and spending on AI have created what 21Shares calls an "AI black hole," drawing money toward the sector and away from assets like Bitcoin and gold. But Bitcoin remains "joined at the hip" with tech stocks, according to Beauchamp. That leaves it in an awkward position: It faces competition for investment dollars when enthusiasm for AI runs high, yet can get dragged down when that enthusiasm fades.  
Fast Company points out Bitcoin "remains down more than 20% since the beginning of 2026."
[Nvidia] has seen its shares lose more than 27% of their value over the past month.  The tech sell-off seems to have dragged down the crypto markets, too, as the two sectors are, on some levels, intermingled... On top of that, outflows from Bitcoin funds may also be contributing to the slide. More than $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions were closed in recent days, which may have added to declining demand, affecting BTC prices.

articles.title: Rachelle Hampton won’t admit how long she spent charting the use of ‘murmur’ in Twilight
articles.body:
Rachelle Hampton is a writer and co-owner at Defector Media, and the host of Normal Gossip, a podcast of anonymous listener-submitted stories about everyday drama. Whether that’s lies about luxury wool in a literal knitting circle, the impeachment of a hypocritical HOA president, or a COVID outbreak at a destination wedding with an absurd 25 bridesmaids, each story is unique in its absurdity, yet weirdly relatable.
Rachelle Hampton won’t admit how long she spent charting the use of ‘murmur’ in Twilight
Normal Gossip host Rachelle Hampton is obsessed with I Like to Watch and splurges on good butter.
Rachelle Hampton won’t admit how long she spent charting the use of ‘murmur’ in Twilight
Normal Gossip host Rachelle Hampton is obsessed with I Like to Watch and splurges on good butter.
After years as one of the co-hosts of Slate’s In Case You Missed It, a podcast that required her to be chronically online, Hampton is enjoying being a little more unplugged these days. And she has perhaps the most interesting answer we’ve ever received to the question “what’s worth splurging on?”
What is your most indispensable tool (analog or digital, app or hardware)?
I think it has to be the Notes app. My entire life is in there! My relationship to the Notes app definitely changes depending on what’s going on in my life at the time. Sometimes I just use it to make my grocery lists, but there was also a period of time where I used it to house my weekly to-do list, so it was basically the only thing between me and destruction. I’ve started blog drafts in the Notes app, and I’ve used it to write out particularly fraught text messages. There are recipes I’ve developed in there, as well as passwords and also questions for my doctors. The first note in my phone is from 2018, so it also serves as a nearly decade-long journal, though there are definitely notes that I simply can’t decipher, like why do I have a note from July 2020 that just says “4th floor”?
Which is the most underappreciated?
I absolutely hate texting. (I write all day, I don’t want to do it in my free time!!) But as someone who also refuses to delete their texts, I have to acknowledge that my most significant personal archive is probably in my Messages inbox.
What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?
It’s a tie between Spotify and whatever phone game I’m currently addicted to, which for the last two years has been Township. I’ve never played Sims or Animal Crossing, but I’m told that it’s something like that. I just like planting my little crops.
How many tabs do you have open right now?
I maintain inbox zero across my entire digital life, so I close all my tabs after I finish a task. Right now I have three tabs that I will close immediately after finishing this questionnaire: the first is the Google Doc I’m typing in, the second is the landing page for this series, and the third is a Google tab where I just searched Animal Crossing to make sure I had the name right.
Which social media platform do you use the most?
It’s a tie between Reddit and YouTube. Hosting a twice-weekly podcast about the internet for three years either gave me some sort of PTSD or cured me of my social media addiction, depending on how you want to look at it. I can’t spend more than twenty minutes max on IG or X or Bluesky without feeling claustrophobic. The exception is when I’m sick, and I let my fever brain rot on IG reels. Otherwise, it just feels like too much information from too many different sources. Reddit and YouTube are both places where I feel somewhat in control of what I’m seeing.
What is your happy place online?
I don’t think I’ve ever been as happy online as I was on Tumblr between 2013 and 2016. I’m always subconsciously chasing that high.
What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?
My older brother bought me a tabletop Klipsch Bluetooth speaker for Christmas a couple of years ago, and it’s still going strong. The sound quality is incredible, and the design is super sexy, so it doesn’t immediately read as a Bluetooth speaker, which I love. I hope I never have to replace it.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
One of the stances I’m proudest of is that I’ve never (intentionally) used ChatGPT or Midjourney or any of the other generative AI tools / large language models. It’s getting harder and harder to avoid now that Gemini is built into Google and its various products. Stop trying to write my emails, Gemini!! I’ve never been swayed away from my belief that every single AI company owes a bankrupting amount of money to the writers and artists whose work their products are built on. Until that debt is paid, there’s nothing appealing to me about talking to a chatbot or creating a shitty poster.
What creation are you most proud of?
In 2020, when I was a staff writer at Slate, I spent a [redacted amount of time] methodically charting and ranking all 349 times Stephenie Meyer used the word murmur in her iconic Twilight saga. The idea had been germinating somewhere in the recesses of my brain for over a decade, only to be released by the surprise 2020 release of Midnight Sun. Seeing this blog come to life (shout out Slate’s interactive designer Natalie Matthews-Ramo!) felt like a fever dream come true.
What is your current obsession?
I’ve rewatched every episode of Netflix’s I Like to Watch with drag queens Trixie Mattel and Katya an embarrassing amount of times. There are certain episodes, like this one where Trixie and Katya react to Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, that I can quote front to back.
What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?
I wish I could say something chill and zen like take a cold shower or something, but the truth is when I’m writing and feeling stuck, I usually smoke a little weed, preferably a sativa strain. Getting high gets me out of my own way, which is usually the problem when I’m feeling stuck. It particularly helps with scriptwriting for Normal Gossip because the tone is so conversational, so being a little bit high stops me from over-writing.
When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?
My favorite coffee shop is less than 500 ft from my apartment, so I end up there without my phone at least once a week, either on purpose or by accident.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
Butter! With the caveat that I live by myself and don’t bake, so butter lasts a while in my household, but good butter can change a whole meal. It makes eating toast feel like a luxury instead of a chore to be completed between meetings because I’ve forgotten to eat lunch. My floor for butter is Kerrygold, but recently I’ve been loving this French brand called Isigny Sainte-Mère.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
Last to arrive, first to leave.
What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

articles.title: Clice v1.0 Released: Welcome to Modern C++
articles.body:
clice recently hit 1,000 commits, a special milestone for the project. Since July 19, 2026, clice has been shipping nightly builds and going through roughly four months of alpha testing, with a huge number of bugs fixed thanks to real-world feedback from early users. Over the same stretch, I built a rigorous testing system for clice and ran extensive tests across many real open-source projects, tracking down and fixing the issues they uncovered. What does that mean? Every core feature is now stable, and you rarely run into problems in day-to-day use. So I think the time is right to ship the first stable release. The project looks very different today from where it stood two years ago in Design and Implementation of a New C++ Language Server, and this is probably the first time I’m promoting it widely, so please let me introduce it to you once again! This is the project I have poured the past two and a half years into, the work I am proudest of, the one that has excited me the most and left me sad and anxious more times than I can count, and the most ambitious thing I have taken on in my short life.
What is clice?
In short, clice is a C/C++ language server written in modern C++, but it’s more than just a language server. It is still built on LLVM/Clang, but unlike clangd and ccls, which are also Clang-based, clice was redesigned from the ground up to fix architectural problems that have gone unsolved in those servers for years. It is written entirely in C++23 and serves as an example of modern C++ best practices in its own right, with all the major modern C++ features coming together remarkably well:
- Written entirely with C++20 coroutines, using our own libuv-based structured-concurrency async library for intricate asynchronous logic. It is a complex concurrent program running an event loop on the main thread while coordinating both multiple processes (IPC) and multiple threads.
- Written entirely with C++20 named modules and C++23 import std, and fully self-hosted: module wrappers for third-party libraries are generated automatically by clice modularize, and clice runs smoothly on its own codebase to provide module-aware language services.
- Uses static reflection built on templates and C++20 concepts for all serialization and deserialization across formats, including TOML, JSON, bincode, blob, and command-line arguments, with Rust-macro-like declarative annotations and zero boilerplate.
- Data-oriented code design throughout, with almost no virtual functions outside the callback interfaces Clang requires. Makes heavy use of modern C++ APIs like std::format, std::expected, std::ranges, and std::views, steering clear of outdated legacy C++98/11 APIs.
- A completely hermetic, reproducible build powered by Bazel, compiled with the unified xclang toolchain for a consistent cross-platform cross-compilation workflow. Compiled binaries are heavily optimized (PGO + LTO), and build artifacts depend on nothing beyond system libraries.
People are always debating whether modern C++ features like modules are actually ready for real work. clice’s answer is: yes, of course, completely usable! They hold up for complex software like clice, with hundreds of thousands of lines of code. Maybe this is what the modern C++ we have been hoping for looks like. That said, the surrounding ecosystem really is inconvenient enough right now that getting this whole workflow running end to end took a huge amount of effort on my part to track issues and adapt everything.
Language Server
Here is an overview of clice’s main features:
- Multi-process compilation: clice compiles code in a process pool modeled after modern web browsers, whereas clangd uses multithreading. Why multiple processes? Because C++ is simply too complex, and on certain corner cases the compiler can easily crash or leak memory. That is especially true for incomplete code in the middle of editing: a huge downstream user base tests compilers on complete code, while very few people test them on half-written code, where the compiler mostly falls back on best-effort heuristics. In clangd, a compiler crash takes down the whole server and forces a restart. In clice, compilation happens in isolated child processes: losing one worker does not affect the rest of the server, so go-to-definition, highlighting, and other services keep working. It also makes it much easier to manage memory usage and schedule compilation priorities, cutting down on unnecessary resource consumption.
- Modules and shared caching: clice has full support for C++20 named modules. All you need is a compile_commands.json containing all module files, and clice scans dependencies on its own and lazily builds required modules on demand, regardless of your build system or compiler, with full support for module completion, highlighting, go-to-definition, hover, and more. Built PCHs and PCMs are also cached on local disk for reuse across sessions. By comparison, clangd offers only very limited module support and no persistent cache.
- Compilation context: clice has full support for non-self-contained files, and more generally for the concept of a compilation context. You can explicitly pick the active context of a file: a specific compile command for a source file, or a specific inclusion site for a header. When you open a non-self-contained file, clice detects its context automatically, so it works out of the box. More broadly, it also supports grouping compile commands into build configurations, letting you switch between, say, debug and release.
- Better template support: clice implements a DFS pseudo instantiator that infers what many dependent names resolve to without needing concrete template arguments for a full instantiation. When a template has been instantiated once, clice also draws on that instantiation to power language features, such as completing on auto parameters of a lambda passed to a ranges call. On top of that, clice treats a template as a duck-typed interface and each instantiation as one of its implementations, much like a virtual function and its overrides: Go to Implementation on a dependent call inside a template lists the functions it actually calls across every instantiation, and Find References and Call Hierarchy work the same way.
- Out-of-the-box experience: Most projects need nothing more than a compile_commands.json. clice ships with built-in environment probing for 50+ toolchains, covering nvcc, MSYS2, Cygwin, zigcc, and more, automatically handling mismatches between your actual compiler and Clang. You don’t have to manually add piles of compiler flags to a config file the way you do with clangd.
Beyond these main features, clice also fixes a long list of smaller clangd issues that have gone untouched for years across semantic highlighting, folding, hover, and more. If you’re interested, give it a try and see what surprises you find. Overall, clice surpasses clangd in ease of use, feature support, and performance. You can install the clice extension in VS Code and other editors and start using it right now.
Command Line
Besides running as a language server, clice can also be used from the CLI to access its language features directly. Currently supported subcommands include:
- clice index: Builds a persistent index for the entire project ahead of time and supports resuming interrupted runs, so your editor starts warm as soon as you open the project.
- clice lint: Built-in clang-tidy runner that checks translation units concurrently across a process pool and merges duplicate diagnostics from headers; pass --index to reuse the same parse pass to build the index along the way.
- clice format: A wrapper around clang-format that automatically finds files to format from your config file or CDB and formats them efficiently in parallel.
- clice command: Shows the effective compile command for a file after rule rewrites and toolchain probing, or converts compile_commands.json into resolved -cc1 commands for other Clang tools.
- clice query: Reads the on-disk index directly without starting a server and outputs symbol definitions, references, call graphs, inheritance hierarchies, and file dependencies as JSON.
- clice refactor: Rewrites source files directly from the persistent index without recompiling, supporting project-wide symbol and macro renaming as well as batch renames in one pass via --spec.
- clice analyze: Outputs project-structure JSON from the index to guide refactoring; for example, analyze modules analyzes module dependencies and cycles across directories and lists code patterns that stand in the way of modularization.
- clice modularize: Automatically wraps third-party libraries used by a project as C++20 modules without modifying any source files; following the split analyze proposes, it can also rewrite the project’s own code into module units, turning headers into partitions and #include into import. clice used it to modularize itself.
The story behind it
That wraps up the feature tour. Next, I want to talk about the story behind the project, some of its design decisions, and my own thoughts and struggles along the way, especially now, in the age of AI.
Why not improve clangd?
First, why start a new project instead of improving clangd? That is the question I get asked most often. There are several reasons. I discussed some of them in my earliest post, and today those problems are even easier to see firsthand:
- Maintenance and staffing: At root, clangd has been effectively unmaintained since around 2024. That sounds surprising. How could a tool used by hundreds of thousands of developers have no one maintaining it? I stumbled onto this fact in 2024 when I was getting ready to submit a PR to clangd for better code completion inside templates. From what I understand, it ties back to a shift in Google’s C++ strategy. Before that, clangd was maintained mainly by several Google engineers, and around 2024 Google started scaling back its investment in C++ (Clang); clangd was deemed good enough for Google’s internal needs, and those engineers were reassigned elsewhere. Since then, clangd has lacked any real long-term maintainers. Only Nathan Ridge has been answering questions unpaid in his spare time, purely out of passion, and one person only has so much bandwidth, making it nearly impossible to handle large PRs. That is why clangd’s C++20 modules PR dragged on for nearly a year, and even today it still isn’t really usable on large projects, with plenty of flaws and nobody working on them. Earlier this year, in 2026, Clang’s lead maintainer Aaron Ballman recognized the problem and posted a call for help on the community forum, saying clangd is very close to unmaintained, with a heavy backlog of PRs and issues, and hoping to find new community maintainers; otherwise clangd could eventually be removed from the LLVM project.
- Scale of the code changes: As mentioned at the start, clice introduces many new architectural ideas, such as multi-process compilation. Implementing those inside clangd would come close to rewriting clangd. Nobody is going to review and accept changes of that size. Self-hosting with modules would also require sweeping changes to LLVM’s build system, which I will go into in detail when I introduce xclang later.
- LLVM repository constraints: clice relies on a lot of third-party libraries for better performance and user experience, such as libuv, simdjson, and tomlplusplus. To keep builds simple, LLVM requires the repository to remain self-contained, so pulling in that many third-party libraries is out of the question. You would either have to rewrite and port them into LLVM or put up with worse ergonomics and lower performance. On top of that, a language server is not a standalone project: it also includes extensions and adapters for different editors. Keeping them in the same repo as the server makes maintenance much easier, and LLVM would be just as unlikely to accept that editor code (spanning Rust, Lua, TypeScript, and so on). For long-term maintainability and our core goals, a separate repository was unavoidable.
So in mid-2024, I started looking into how to design and write a new language server. At the end of 2024, I published Design and Implementation of a New C++ Language Server, setting out clice’s core goals and kicking off development in earnest.
How did we get here?
Next, let’s talk about how clice was built. How did it get to its current state? Over the past two and a half years, at a rough guess, I have put nearly 3,000 hours into this project. Even that number doesn’t really tell the story, because clice became part of my life. It was always on my mind, like eating or sleeping: there wasn’t a moment when I wasn’t turning over some problem related to it. Development broke down into roughly four stages:
Mid-2024 to early 2025: I spent this period studying Clang and clangd’s codebase and internals. Anyone who has looked through my older blog posts will know I am a longtime template metaprogramming enthusiast, familiar with C++ and its implementation details down to language-lawyer territory. During this phase I settled on clice’s core goals and overall design, and put together an initial demo. I was a third-year undergrad at the time: I would wake up and start coding right away, skip lunch, walk out to the McDonald’s outside the campus gate when I got hungry, and put in 8 to 10 hours a day.
Early 2025 to early 2026: I originally expected to ship a usable version of clice fairly quickly during this stage. Instead, progress went much slower than I expected, and it remained a long way from production-ready. Looking back, there were a few main reasons:
- Above all, time. I had assumed I would keep putting in 8 to 10 hours a day like before. My undergraduate major was chemistry, though, and everything I knew about programming was self-taught. Even though I had plenty of C++ experience and had participated in GSoC, I lacked specific “domain knowledge.” To find a job, I spent most of 2025 interning and picking up a new field (unrelated to C++ frontends), while also dealing with university chores and everything involved in graduating. The hours I had left for clice shrank drastically compared to my earlier assumptions, so progress naturally slowed down.
- Getting the project genuinely production-ready also took far more than the core architecture. It meant working through countless corner cases of C++ syntax alongside subtle cross-platform differences: URI parsing, file paths and file uniqueness, OS-level quirks, and so on. The workload turned out to be much bigger than I had imagined. I also have a bit of an obsessive streak and dislike band-aid solutions that barely get by, so to build things the way I wanted I ended up reinventing quite a few wheels, covering serialization, IPC/LSP, async, and more. Had I chosen Rust at the start, development might have taken considerably less time, since those pieces already existed in the Rust ecosystem and had been thoroughly proven in other language servers. Still, writing a C++ language server in Rust felt odd, and it would have ruled out self-hosting, so I didn’t go that route.
- Lack of experience scheduling and managing complex software. Even with so much work on the table, several early contributors were already interested in the project and willing to put real time into helping write code. Unfortunately, I had very little teamwork experience back then (being completely self-taught and only three years into programming altogether), so I failed to turn that interest into effective contributions. That sank in much deeper once I started working in industry: 3 or 4 of my coworkers can split up responsibilities, stand up a project from scratch in 2 to 3 months, and ship it to production, whereas I had poor instincts for project planning and mostly just wrote whatever was on my mind at the moment. Open-source volunteer bandwidth can’t be compared to a full-time job, of course, yet the truth is I didn’t do a great job of building a community or pushing the project forward.
Early 2026 to July 2026: The turning point came when coding agents led by Claude Opus 4.6 started catching on. I began using agents to help with the mountain of tedious detail work and painful cross-platform debugging, and found they were remarkably good at it. During this stretch I did a sweeping cleanup of the existing codebase and established the prototype of clice as it stands today. As agents grew stronger, I handed them increasingly complex tasks and kept moving the project forward rapidly. It was an exciting period: I could finally stop burning hours on tedious details and focus on architecture and feature work. At the same time, it hit me that coding agents were only going to keep getting stronger. If humans stop writing code altogether in the future, what point does a language server even have? That pushed me to start designing and building clice’s CLI features.
July 2026 to present: By July I felt the timing was right to put out early test builds and iterate based on real user feedback. Core language server features were already in place and fully usable day to day, though still short of everything I had originally envisioned, so I threw myself into building out the rest of that vision, tuning performance, and fixing bugs. In October, I started planning clice’s modular self-hosting. That was a remarkably complicated undertaking, because C++ module support today is a long, painful story:
- CMake supports modules, yet if implementation units importing a module use different compile flags, CMake forks a separate compilation of the module even when those flags don’t affect PCM compatibility. CMake also has no built-in compilation cache, which matters a lot for CI; normally we reach for ccache to solve that, except ccache doesn’t support modules.
- clice has a demanding platform matrix: six combinations across Windows/Linux/macOS × ARM64/x64, plus ASan builds, prebuilt LLVM/Clang binaries to speed up CI, C++23 import std, and build artifacts that depend only on system libraries rather than extra shared libraries so everything works out of the box for users.
I surveyed the options extensively, and the answer was that an out-of-the-box setup for this simply did not exist in open source, and most open-source C++ module projects don’t have build requirements nearly this involved. After thinking it through carefully, I built xclang, inspired by zigcc, to give every target platform a unified cross-compilation experience, and paired it with Bazel (which includes built-in build caching) to solve the build problem for good. Going one step further, I wrote clice modularize to automatically generate module wrappers for every third-party library we depend on, completing clice’s self-hosted modularization! That probably makes clice one of the most complex open-source C++ projects using modules today.
Alongside all of this, I ran extensive fuzz testing across many open-source projects and fixed a huge number of bugs, bringing clice to genuine production readiness!
What about agents?
As I mentioned earlier, I designed a CLI interface for clice so that it would still hold some value in the agent era. An obvious idea is replacing grep with clice query: it is more accurate and uses fewer tokens. That is true, except exact symbol lookup requires indexing the whole project first, which takes a very long time. grep is imprecise, sure, yet 2 or 3 grep calls are usually enough to find the target, and the extra text grep pulls back isn’t necessarily a bad thing for helping an agent understand the codebase. Put plainly, most of this CLI isn’t actually all that useful. The part that really earns its keep is probably clice modularize: if you ask an agent to modularize a project on its own, it spins up a swarm of subagents and writes custom scripts to pull off the migration, which is both slow and expensive. Giving the agent clice modularize to assist the migration works much better. LLMs are trained first and foremost for generality, and what they do best is writing and combining scripts to generalize across problems. As things stand, only highly specialized tools still carry real value; otherwise you are usually better off letting the LLM compose its own scripts.
As agents keep getting stronger, especially with models led by Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2, the cost of building complex software keeps falling, and 10x or even 100x the productivity of the past is well within reach. Over on X, you can see plenty of people asking Claude in a single sentence to rewrite the TypeScript compiler in another programming language and getting better performance out of it. Surprising at first glance, yet completely reasonable when you think about it. Software written in the past was bounded by human time, cost, and skill, so codebases inevitably accumulated lots of suboptimal code paths. When humans optimize performance, we go after the main bottlenecks, whereas an agent can tirelessly optimize every path until the small wins add up. Refactoring also often produces a better architecture than existing code; rewriting or refactoring software was just too expensive to justify before. In the foreseeable future, then, most code may be written entirely by agents, humans may stop writing code and even reading it (which is already happening now), and language servers may have no reason to exist at all. Agents might even invent programming languages better suited to themselves: compilation and interpretation themselves have often become the bottleneck in the agent loop, and agents already have the ability to optimize that underlying infrastructure; they just haven’t started yet. Ideally, every stage of the agent loop should be something the agent itself can improve and speed up, compilers and toolchains included.
To be continued
That is a sad reality, and in an era like this it means the effort I poured into clice over the past two and a half years is unlikely to have the lasting meaning I first imagined. Every time I dwell on it, I slip into a dark mood, bordering on nihilism. I can’t help asking myself: thousands of hours and a lot of money, and what was it all for?
Because I taught myself programming off the beaten path without a CS degree, I got used early on to the cycle of finding my own goals, defining problems, solving them, and then looking for the next goal. Interest alone only sustains me for a little while; sticking with something for the long haul takes some deeper “meaning” or “vision” behind it, ideally one I defined for myself. And now that meaning is fading away. So over the past few months, I started pushing myself relentlessly. The more those thoughts crept in, the harder I used agents to drive the project forward, trying to finish it before it lost its meaning altogether.
Imagine an alternate timeline where coding agents never took off. clice wouldn’t be nearly as complete as it is today, of course, yet I would have slowly gained experience, learned how to collaborate and plan work, built a community around it, and watched clice move forward slowly and steadily. Except the SOTA models have already been trained. Models like Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 are real, and whether AI is a bubble or not, they aren’t going away. Software becoming cheap is already an undeniable fact.
We have to face reality, so what mindset should we bring to all of this? My thinking has shifted again recently, though honestly neither my mental state nor my daily life is in a great place right now. Pouring yourself too deeply into one thing naturally takes a heavy toll when it doesn’t turn out the way you hoped. Still, if you zoom out over a longer stretch of time, what does it really amount to? Even if I had done nothing at all for these two and a half years, so what? There is plenty of life ahead. I know that in principle, yet letting go is hard, especially when this project has been part of my life for over two years. As I mentioned in an earlier post, graduating from college never really felt real to me, because the rhythm of my life barely changed afterward: apart from my job, it was just this project. Something has to change eventually, though. I can treat clice as my graduation project: my real graduation project, not one from the chemistry major I never really liked. And that’s enough. I don’t need to force a grander meaning onto it. This graduation project has met every single goal I set two years ago, and exceeded them by a wide margin. It stands on its own as the best illustration of modern C++, neatly bringing together everything I studied about C++ in college. If on top of that it can be helpful to people just learning to program or curious about modern C++, that is plenty.
So this post is a kind of ritual for me. I need to step out of my old life and look for other things worth doing, maybe things outside code. I will keep maintaining clice, just not at the intensity I used to; practically everything worth building is already built anyway, so from here on it will mostly be incremental optimizations and bug fixes based on user feedback. In times like these, it is hard to say what the right path is, or what you ought to be doing. Nobody knows what will happen next week, let alone next year, or how far AI will actually go. I think it is time to rest for a while so I don’t burn out, and have the energy to face whatever problems come next. I still have a strong drive to keep creating good work. It just might not be about programming anymore, and figuring that out is what I need to learn and think through in this next stage.
That’s all for this post. Thanks for reading. I hope you’ll give clice a try, and feel free to report any problems!

articles.title: What Picasso taught me about building AI Agents
articles.body:
The great master Pablo Picasso is famously attributed with saying:
"It took me four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child."
His work, Le Taureau (The Bull), captures this beautifully. Across 11 iterations, Picasso progressively stripped away the details of a bull until only a few lines remained. Yet the bull was unmistakable.
In my journey of learning to build AI agents, I can relate. It has come full circle.
Like many engineers, I started with abstractions and sophisticated software systems. Frameworks, orchestration engines, multi-agent architectures, state machines, vector databases, memory systems, and elaborate planning mechanisms.
The more I experimented, the more I found myself stripping things away.
The models were getting better. More things worked with a single prompt. But that wasn't the whole story. I had been overcomplicating things.
This is now my workflow.
I open my terminal.
mkdir my_awesome_agent
cd my_awesome_agent
claude
and start a conversation.
"Claude, I want to build an agent that does XYZ. Help me initialize it. Create an AGENTS.md and let's figure out what else it needs."
I work through a few questions with Claude.
What is this agent supposed to accomplish?
What is the actual job? Not what framework to use, unless you're creating a framework. What does success look like? What decisions can the agent make independently? What should it never do without permission?
What skills does it need?
Skills are specialized instructions that can be reused and remixed. There are plenty of excellent examples on the internet. Borrow them, adapt them, combine them, or ask Claude to create new ones.
Often, a skill is simply a Markdown file with instructions and perhaps a few supporting resources.
What context does it need?
The agent will need context: what your business does, who your customers are, how your codebase works, or some domain-specific knowledge. These can all live as Markdown files inside the folder. Some context can be retrieved when needed. Some comes from the conversation itself. You don't automatically need a vector database or a sophisticated memory architecture.
What tools does it need?
To perform a job, an agent needs tools. Maybe it needs to search the web, read a database, call an API, execute a script, or interact with a browser.
Introducing a tool is as simple as enabling a plugin or adding an MCP connector.
I ask Claude to help identify the smallest set of tools required to accomplish the task. A tool could even be created dynamically, with the agent writing and invoking code. The agent could also find tools on the internet and install them.
How does the agent get invoked?
For an agent to be useful, it needs to be invoked as part of a workflow, whether by a cron job, a webhook event, or another program.
The simplicity is in the packaging. A folder with instructions is a clean deployable unit. It can be versioned, copied around, and embedded in other processes.
With Claude and the required tools and credentials available, it can be invoked headless using the -p flag:
cd my_awesome_agent
claude -p "Do awesome stuff"
Headless means there is no interactive chat. Claude receives the task, works in the agent's folder, prints the result, and exits. A script can pass in the task and collect the output. For unattended work, I configure the tool permissions in advance. Claude can also return structured JSON for another program to use.
Anthropic's documentation on headless execution covers the commands and configuration.
When the agent starts, it needs to know where to find its instructions, what input it has received, and whether it should resume previous work. The invocation mechanism can change without changing the fundamental purpose of the agent.
This setup can be deployed on a remote VM, with hooks triggering the agent and a tunnel providing access to a service that invokes it.
How does it know whether it has done a good job?
This is where things have drastically improved. I can now get things done with a single prompt, without elaborate instructions. Nowadays, I often just trust it to get on with the job. And I expect it to keep getting better.
When it gets something wrong, I go through it with Claude. What happened? What was missing? What should we change?
Claude saves local session transcripts under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>.jsonl. Each transcript records the conversation, tool calls, and tool results. It provides a trace of how the task unfolded: what Claude was asked to do, what it tried, what came back from the tools, and where errors appeared.
Claude can then be pointed at the transcript and asked to analyze the run. Where did it go off track? Did it miss an instruction, lack context, or misinterpret a tool result? What evidence in the trace supports that explanation? That gives us something concrete to examine before deciding what to change.
If the lesson is reusable, we save it in the instructions, context, examples, or tests.
Over time, the agent improves. Not necessarily because its underlying model has changed, but because its working context and operating instructions have become better.
How do we know it is improving?
To be rigorous about the implementation, you need benchmarks: representative tasks with clear criteria for success. Running the same tasks lets you compare your agent across harnesses such as Gemini CLI, Codex, or pi, or across models such as Opus, Astra, Sol, and DeepSeek. It also tells you whether changes to your own setup are helping.
These tests are called evals. This is probably the hardest part of all of this. I will share my experiences with evals in a later post. In the meantime, these writeups explain them in much more depth:
- Hugo Bowne-Anderson: Does Your AI Agent Actually Work? A Guide to Evals
- Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar: AI Evals: Everything You Need to Know
Orchestration
A task can be broken into smaller tasks and delegated to specialized subagents. In this setup, each subagent has its own folder under the main agent, containing its instructions, context, and tools.
The root agent acts as an orchestrator, or chief of staff. It decides which subagent to invoke, gives it a task, and brings the results together. For example, a chief-of-staff agent could coordinate all kinds of activity across a company, delegating work to specialist agents.
Making this concrete
I am using this setup to publish this website, including the article you are reading. For this project, I am using Codex.
The agent works in the website's project folder. AGENTS.md points it to my editorial guidance and publishing instructions. Those files capture my preferences and the steps for updating the site. Here is a shortened view of the actual folder:
claramap/
├── AGENTS.md
├── docs/
│   ├── editorial-memory.md
│   └── publishing.md
├── content/posts/
│   └── what-picasso-taught-me-about-building-ai-agents.md
├── public/assets/blog/
└── scripts/
    ├── build.mjs
    └── check-live.mjs
The agent is connected to Cloudflare through MCP, so it can deploy the site as part of the workflow.
For this article, I asked it to add the orchestration section and create the chief-of-staff diagram. It edited the Markdown, generated the illustration, built the site, deployed to Cloudflare, and checked the live page.
The publishing instructions also cover Google Analytics and discovery files. The build automatically updates the site's analytics tracking code for its current pages, regenerates llms.txt and llms-full.txt, and updates the RSS feed.
I review the result and correct it in the same conversation. Change the wording. Move a diagram. Make an image bigger. Reusable feedback goes back into the editorial memory, so future runs have better instructions to work with.
The Essence
This is the foundation. Everything else builds on this.
No need for OpenClaw, Hermes, Muse, LangChain, Pydantic, or any other agent framework. Solve the basic case first, then add machinery later. You can find leads, create content, publish, send emails, answer questions, fill out forms, or write code. Pick a job. Give it what it needs. Let it work.
Like Picasso's bull, my approach became simpler as I learned what to leave out. The progression looks something like this.
