articles.title: Congress wants to tighten export rules on AI chips after Nvidia spy scandal
articles.body:
Unsurprisingly, following the scandal involving now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, Congress is looking to further restrict exports of AI chips. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for various measures and bills that would tighten rules and have demanded that Huang and other Nvidia leaders testify before Congress.
Congress wants to tighten export rules on AI chips after Nvidia spy scandal
Following revelations about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy Congress wants to crack down.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already said that Huang and the Trump administration need to answer to Congress. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has also sent letters to both Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick calling on them to publicly testify to the committee.
Bills such as the Remote Access Security Act, first introduced in the House in April 2025 but stalled in the Senate, are receiving renewed interest. While that specific bill might not become law, House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is “growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China,” according to Reuters. Johnson has also said that he personally supports efforts to restrict China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

articles.title: Court denies motion to dismiss DRAM price fixing case
articles.body:
Key Points
- Judge Noël Wise denied in full Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron's joint motion to dismiss a proposed class action alleging they conspired to cut supply of conventional DRAM, such as DDR5, and shift capacity to HBM.
- The court held the case was not a rerun of DRAM II, the Ninth Circuit's 2022 affirmance of dismissal of an earlier DRAM conspiracy suit against the same companies.
- The judge found that long-term HBM lock-ups, refusals of long-term conventional DRAM contracts, Micron's Crucial closure, fab delays, the failure to expand despite record prices, near-identical customer vetting and the companies' prior cartel history supported a plausible inference of conspiracy.
- The court gave no weight to three of the plaintiffs' arguments: investor statements about "supply discipline," which it found too similar to statements the Ninth Circuit's DRAM II decision had already held insufficient; executives' meetings at industry conferences, since DRAM II all but forecloses relying on them unless plaintiffs identify what was actually exchanged or agreed there; and the three-company market structure, which it called neutral.
- Answers are due Dec. 7, 2026, and the initial case management conference was reset for Jan. 12, 2027.
A federal judge on Nov. 14 refused to dismiss a proposed class action accusing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron of conspiring to restrict the supply of conventional dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, the standardized memory chips used in computers, phones and servers.
U.S. District Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California denied the companies' joint motion to dismiss in full, finding the complaint plausibly alleged an agreement in violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The allegations, accepted as true at this stage, have not been proven.
The companies argued the case was a rerun of DRAM II, in which the Ninth Circuit in 2022 affirmed dismissal of claims against the same three companies over a 2016–2018 supply restriction. "The Court finds that it is not," Judge Wise wrote.
The suit was filed June 25, 2026, by 17 consumers and small businesses from five states. It concerns conventional DRAM, which the complaint describes as "standardized memory built to industry specifications and sold for ordinary purposes," including DDR5 generation modules built for computers.
According to the complaint, the three companies controlled more than 91% of global DRAM revenue as of the third quarter of 2025. They allegedly cut production starting in late 2022 and, beginning in 2023, shifted capacity to high bandwidth memory, or HBM, a specialized DRAM product for artificial intelligence accelerators that "requires approximately three to four times the silicon wafer area per gigabyte compared to conventional DDR5 DRAM."
By the third quarter of 2025, conventional DRAM prices had risen 171.8% in one year, according to the complaint, which alleges a 697% increase over 18 months. Yet "not one of the three Defendants expanded or announced plans to meaningfully expand commodity DRAM production capacity," the complaint alleges.
Without direct evidence of an agreement, the plaintiffs needed plus factors, additional facts suggesting a preceding agreement rather than conscious parallelism, in which competitors independently make similar moves.
Judge Wise rejected the companies' argument that timing gaps undercut parallel action. SK Hynix and Micron announced cuts three weeks apart in late 2022, she noted, and Samsung's lag of about four and a half months, until April 7, 2023, was "not such an unreasonably long delay that it defeats an allegation of parallel conduct on a motion to dismiss."
She found the complaint plausibly alleged that the three companies acted in parallel when they cut supply, shifted production from conventional DRAM such as DDR5 to HBM, and wound down DDR4.
Under Ninth Circuit precedent, action against self-interest must be "so perilous in the absence of advance agreement that no reasonable firm would make the challenged move without such an agreement." Judge Wise wrote that a pivot to HBM by itself "might not be sufficient," but that "the related conduct tips this factor over the edge to weigh in Plaintiffs' favor."
According to the complaint, all three signed long-term contracts locking in HBM supply, Samsung and SK Hynix reportedly refused long-term agreements with major conventional DRAM customers, and Micron announced on Dec. 3, 2025, that it would close Crucial, its 30-year-old consumer brand. Those moves, which she called "difficult if not impossible to unwind," plus the failure to expand despite record prices, "are the sort that at the pleading stage, it appears no reasonable firm would make without a prior agreement," she wrote.
She applied similar reasoning to allegations that Samsung and Micron delayed or halted new DRAM plants, citing the Ninth Circuit's 1990 Petroleum Products decision that "Changes in refinery capacity are not readily reversible." "The Court views the commitment to build or not build manufacturing capacity as analogous," she wrote. She also counted the companies' alleged same-quarter 2025 decisions to wind down DDR4 as a plus factor, citing the complaint's allegation that "older, slower DDR4 came to cost more per gigabyte than newer, faster DDR5."
Judge Wise found that near-identical customer-vetting practices all three companies allegedly adopted in January 2026 "strongly support a plausible inference of conspiracy." She rejected the companies' "obvious and non-conspiratorial explanation" of booming AI demand, noting that the vetting began after the AI boom and the HBM pivot were underway.
The court gave no weight to three other arguments. Judge Wise held that investor statements, including Micron's 2022 reference to "supply discipline," did not distinguish the case from DRAM II. Though the conference-meeting allegations went beyond those in DRAM II, she wrote that DRAM II "seemingly all but forecloses a trial court from giving any weight to trade conference meetings" absent specifics, and she called the market's oligopolistic structure "neutral in the analysis."
According to the complaint, the companies and two other manufacturers formed a criminal cartel to fix DRAM prices from 1998 to 2002; Samsung paid a $300 million fine, Hynix paid $185 million, and Micron received immunity for cooperating as a whistleblower. Judge Wise, like the DRAM II court, rejected the argument that the now-20-year-old history should not count.
At the hearing, the companies quoted the late Judge Posner's line that competitors in concentrated markets "watch each other like hawks." Judge Wise wrote: "But Plaintiffs' allegations go beyond hawks watching each other; their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do."
The plaintiffs are represented by Bathaee Dunne LLP. Samsung is represented by O'Melveny & Myers LLP, SK Hynix by Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP, and Micron by Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP.
Judge Wise ordered the companies to answer by Dec. 7, 2026. Because the court had reset argument by about three weeks, she also granted the companies' unopposed administrative motion to continue early case deadlines and reset the initial case management conference for Jan. 12, 2027, at 9 a.m.

articles.title: We're Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches
articles.body:
Today, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.
Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places.
But ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin, ALPRs give law enforcement “a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment.
We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant.

articles.title: 'Birdbrain' Is a Misnomer. Crows Make Decisions Faster Than We Can
articles.body:
Supported by
‘Birdbrain’ Is a Misnomer. Crows Make Decisions Faster Than We Can
In a recent experiment, crows could process and respond to visual cues at twice the speed as humans and monkeys.
Lemmy and Iggy, two carrion crows, are no strangers to a psychology lab. As study participants, they have helped scientists prove that birds can use tools to forage, learn numbers and count objects, and provided other insights into the ways birds think.
Now, they’ve also revealed that birds can make staggeringly quick decisions, besting their human and nonhuman primate counterparts with ease. In new findings published in Science, the crows could process and respond to visual cues at twice the speed as humans and monkeys, quantifying the neural speed of avian decision-making for the first time.
The discovery might be the final blow for the use of “birdbrains” as a pejorative.
“We wouldn’t think of birds making these decisions faster than monkeys, or faster than us ‘awesome’ human beings,” said Mike Colombo, a neuroscientist and comparative psychologist at the University of Otago in New Zealand who was not involved in the research. “But they do. They’re just incredibly fast.”
Questions of bird intelligence have long been debated by researchers. Their small and superficially simple brains led scholars in the 19th and much of the 20th century to conclude they were not cognitively competent creatures. Even early research into birdsong, which demonstrated that some birds are capable of complex speech-like patterns and impressive vocal mimicry, was not enough to turn the tide. Their elaborate melodies were considered specialized adaptations that didn’t reflect their cognitive abilities.
Although passionate birders may find those conclusions obviously mistaken, the scientific community has been slower to catch on. “It’s taken the last 20 years to realize that actually their brain architecture is quite fascinating,” said Dr. Colombo.
Recent research, for example, has found that pigeons are capable of distinguishing between cancerous and noncancerous cells, numerical values, and words and non-words. Corvids (the group that includes crows, ravens, rooks and scrub jays) can even recognize themselves, solve abstract problems, plan for the future and show theory of mind — an ability to understand what other birds might be thinking and act accordingly.

articles.title: Show HN: A tiny macOS app that turns off the MacBook display [free license]
articles.body:
Blackout turns off your MacBook’s built-in display when you are working on an external monitor. System settings will not show the internal display as a desktop anymore. Unplugging monitors or closing the app will return to normal state again.
Use the switches above to see how your displays appear in macOS.
This works perfectly on Apple Silicon Macs (M-series), but on Intel Macs you'll still see the internal display listed on this system preferences page (macOS limitation).
Individual display switches
Switch individual displays on or off from one window.
Keep the lid open
Use your MacBook’s keyboard and trackpad with its screen dark.
Automatic reset to default
If something goes wrong, the app will automatically reset the screens to default (all screens are on)
Minimal footprint
Reduce the app to a tiny top menu bar icon, without an icon in the dock
Detects monitor disconnects
If monitor cable is unplugged, the app will detect this and act accordingly
TouchID keeps working
Unlike other tools, login or authentication via TouchID will work even with the display turned off.
No, as Apple doesn't allow software that uses the Apple hardware API in the App Store, probably to protect normies from breaking their systems. This app is officially signed by Apple with my valid Apple Developer account, so it's safe to use.
What happens when I close the app, restart the Mac, the app crashes, or I unplug the monitor cable?
In all these cases the internal display will be turned on with 80% brightness instantly. Also when macOS updates or other such events happen.
Is this a permanent change?
No, everything is just software-based, so whatever happens, your display will be back online after a macOS restart anyways.
Compatibility
The community is testing many devices, and this table will get updates.
All devices should work. Intel machines and base M3 MacBook / M3 MacBook Air have a hardware bug that MIGHT prevent turning off the internal display.

articles.title: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills, Reports ProPublica
articles.body:
Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills, Reports ProPublica (propublica.org) 36
			
		 	
				Environmental activist Bill Gates has "quietly accumulated a $29 billion stake in America's No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services," reports ProPublica, in a new 5,000-word investigation. But inspectors from America's Environmental Protection Agency "have repeatedly found methane — a highly potent greenhouse gas — escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits.  Republic has lobbied against regulations that could make the waste industry cleaner, including by keeping organic garbage out of landfills in the first place."
While Gates has invested at least $2 billion in green companies, he's "put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry," their article argues. And Gates has increased his stake in Republic "to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion."
While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They're responsible for as much as a fifth of the country's emissions of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports....
[Gates] has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor... "It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic's behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits," said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder... Gates didn't respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn't find any public comments he's made about them.  
But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic's shares — "It's 'Garbage In' for Gates," the New York Post headline read — the company's stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows... A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune [in 1999]... To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he'd given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets... After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates' stake in Republic over the years that followed. [On behalf of the Gates Foundation] Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic's main competitor, Waste Management.
 
Methane emissions weren't a major focus of climate activism until years later
The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and it's responsible for one-third of the global warming we experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. But it also breaks down much more quickly, turning into CO2 and water vapor in about a decade — which means that cutting methane emissions now would reduce that warming within our lifetimes. This is especially urgent, scientists say, as the climate approaches tipping points that could doom rainforests, coral reefs and ice sheets.

articles.body:
Manjaro Linux Moves Toward Independent Community Governance (linuxiac.com) 3
			
		 	
				Arch-based Manjaro Linux "has announced that Manjaro Project e.V. is now officially registered as a non-profit in Germany," reports Linuxiac, "and is therefore a legally separate entity from the commercial Manjaro GmbH & Co. KG... after months of internal wrangling over who was in charge of the project, who had access to the infrastructure and who didn't, and the relationship between the dev team and the commercial company..."
The restructuring goes back to March, when the Manjaro developers released the Manjaro 2.0 Manifesto, which was a very public critique of the way Manjaro was being run.  The document claims that decision-making has effectively become the sole domain of the project founder, Philip Müller, with the other developers having very limited access to the infrastructure. There's also a concern about the drop in participation, the persistent technical issues, and the continued prioritization of commercial interests over the actual development of the distribution...
The manifesto proposed the transfer of all project infrastructure, domains, repositories and community funds to the new organization, together with arrangements for the use of the Manjaro trademark. The contributors were warning that they might well consider forking the distro if the talks didn't go their way. Müller then indicated that he'd be happy to talk about the proposed structure once the non-profit was in place. The association is now formally registered, and so one of the key aims of the manifesto has been realized... 
Perhaps the most important point is the actual evolution of the distribution. The most recent testing and stable updates were kicked off by the Manjaro team themselves, without any oversight from Müller. This points to the developers having already started to operate on their own in an area which was previously the preserve of the project's founder. They're also in the process of optimizing their dev infrastructure, in part as a response to the continued automated bot attacks on the existing infrastructure. 
Thanks to Slashdot reader king*jojo for sharing the news.

articles.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
articles.body:
All AI-generated code should be Open Source
This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.
First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.
The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute, which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain.
However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.
Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.
If you find this article interesting you may want to follow me on Twitter: @jcubic and on LinkedIn.

articles.title: Show HN: Gawain – Require type hints on all Python variables
articles.body:
gawain requires type annotations on the variables, parameters, returns and class attributes of Python code, then runs a type checker, ty or pyrefly, to check that the types are correct.
Type checkers such as mypy, Pyright, ty and pyrefly infer the type of a variable that has no annotation. ruff's ANN
rules and flake8-annotations ask for annotations on functions only. gawain also asks for them on variables and
class attributes.
I built gawain only because I hate dict[str, Any] and wanted to do something about it. If your answer to
this is "but Python already infers that" or "but my IDE infers it for me", then don't use it, little padawan.
Given shop.py:
PORT = 8080
retries = 3
total = compute()
def send(to, body):
    print(f"to {to}: {body}")
class Order:
    def __init__(self, items: list[str]) -> None:
        self.items = items
gawain check shop.py prints:
[presence]
shop.py:1:1    GW001 variable 'PORT' has no type annotation
shop.py:3:1    GW001 variable 'total' has no type annotation
shop.py:6:5    GW003 function 'send' has no return type annotation
shop.py:6:10   GW002 parameter 'to' of function 'send' has no type annotation
shop.py:6:14   GW002 parameter 'body' of function 'send' has no type annotation
shop.py:12:14  GW004 attribute 'items' is not declared in the body of class 'Order'
6 errors (presence). Type check skipped until presence errors are fixed.
retries = 3 passes, because a literal has an obvious type. PORT is a constant, so it needs Final[int].
When every annotation is in place, gawain runs the type checker on the same files and prints what it reports.
With ty, the default, for
prices.py:
def total(prices: list[int]) -> int:
    return "0"[types]
prices.py:2:12  ty[invalid-return-type] Return type does not match returned value: expected `int`, found `Literal["0"]`
1 error (types).
Install gawain with the extra of the type checker you want. ty is the default checker, and the ty extra pins
it to 0.0.100:
uv tool install "gawain[ty]"
# or
pip install "gawain[ty]"
To use pyrefly instead, install the pyrefly extra, which pins pyrefly 1.4.1 and does not install ty:
uv tool install "gawain[pyrefly]"
# or
pip install "gawain[pyrefly]"
Then choose it with checker = "pyrefly" in [tool.gawain], or with --checker pyrefly.
docs/configuration.md
explains the switch.
pip install gawain without an extra installs only the gawain command. It then needs a checker on PATH, or
--no-types to run the annotation checks only.
Warning
Use gawain with care. ty is in beta, and its diagnostics may change between versions. If that is a problem
for your project, use pyrefly, or --no-types to run the annotation checks only.
gawain check src/                  # annotations, then types
gawain check src/ --no-types       # annotations only
gawain check src/ --checker pyrefly  # pyrefly instead of ty
gawain check src/ --mode strict    # an annotation on every assignment
gawain check src/ --format json    # one JSON object, for tools
gawain exits with 0 when nothing is reported, 1 when it reports an error, and 2 on a usage error or
when the type checker cannot run. The type checker's warnings are printed but do not fail the check.
GW000 marks a file gawain cannot read, and GW900 and GW901 mark a broken or unused suppression. To silence a line, name the code:
value = load()  # gawain: ignore[GW001]
docs/rules.md has the full rules, the exemptions and the suppression syntax.
The default mode is obvious. A name may go without an annotation when its value has an obvious type and the
name is never assigned again: a literal (count = 0), a container of literals (ids = [1, 2, 3]) or a
constructor call (user = User("ada")). strict asks for an annotation on every assignment:
[tool.gawain]
mode = "strict"
docs/rules.md has the exact rules of each mode.
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/matheuzgomes/gawain
    rev: v0.3.1
    hooks:
      - id: gawain
pre-commit installs the hook from this repository's source, so building it needs Rust 1.97 or newer.
docs/configuration.md covers [tool.gawain], paths and the hook in detail.
On the CPython 3.14 standard library (1,847 files, 974,586 lines), median of 30 runs (5 for flake8-annotations):
gawain ran with --no-types. This is one benchmark on one machine (AMD Ryzen 7 3700X, WSL2).
docs/benchmarks.md has the versions and the commands to run it again.
- docs/rules.md: rules, modes, exemptions and suppression.
- docs/configuration.md: paths, output, exit codes, [tool.gawain] and pre-commit.
- docs/benchmarks.md: how the numbers above were measured.
gawain reads Python with ruff_python_parser and checks types with ty, both by Astral, or with pyrefly, by Meta.
I don't know, I just like the Arthurian tales. Gawain is a knight of the Round Table, and the mascot is the Green Knight's axe with the green girdle from Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.
MIT. See LICENSE.

articles.title: America Officially Loses Its Measles-elimination Status After Continued Spread of the Disease
articles.body:
America Officially Loses Its Measles-elimination Status After Continued Spread of the Disease (msn.com) 123
			
		 	
				Reuters reports:
The Pan American Health Organization has revoked the United States' measles-elimination status, ending a 26-year run after determining the country failed to halt continuous transmission of the highly contagious virus for more than a year, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday...
The reported decision by the Americas branch of the World Health Organization comes as the US battles the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades. Some 7,500 people in the US have been infected with measles and 13 have died since 2025. That period coincides with falling immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines...
Canada, Spain and the UK recently lost measles-elimination status after review by WHO experts....
"It is a fully preventable disease. It is unconscionable that we have this amount of measles," said Noel Brewer, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina...  William Moss, an epidemiology professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, said loss of measles elimination was a hit to the United States' reputation as a public health powerhouse... For the average American, he added, it means that the United States will continue to have large outbreaks, putting people at risk of disease, hospitalization and death.

articles.title: Italy Fines Meta €805m Over Accessing Android Users' Photos with Facebook App
articles.body:
Italy Fines Meta €805m Over Accessing Android Users' Photos with Facebook App (bbc.com) 29
			
		 	
				The Associated Press reports:
Italy announced an €805 million ($887 million) fine against Meta on Saturday for using photos and videos from Android users' galleries on Facebook without specific consent or adequate disclosure...
Investigators found that the feature was enabled by default and that Facebook requested gallery access through a single permission covering multiple app functions with different purposes. The authority gave Meta 60 days to disable the feature and seek separate consent for its use.  
Italy has about 20 million Android users, notes the BBC, and this fine "is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant."
The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts...  According to the Italian regulator, a preceding [authorization] notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery. The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".  It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation". 
"A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal..."

articles.title: EFF Criticizes US Government's Use of AI For Evaluating Senior Health Insurance Requests
articles.body:
EFF Criticizes US Government's Use of AI For Evaluating Senior Health Insurance Requests (eff.org) 48
			
		 	
				"When we need medical care, we expect decisions about our treatment to be made by our doctors, not a tech company's algorithm," writes the EFF newsletter EFFector.
But in January America's federal government launched a program called WISeR that uses AI to evaluate authorization requests for certain procedures from America's federal health insurance program for seniors, Medicare.  EFF sued for records and discovered "additional issues" with the program that they say "could jeopardize Medicare beneficiaries' access to care."
 The records we received revealed that WISeR has resulted in widespread delays and denials of care, operational chaos, and reports of patient harm. Further documents obtained by EFF show a rushed and rocky rollout, highlighting the dangers that arise when governments treat AI like a silver bullet for complex problems.
EFF has now published hundreds of pages of documents obtained through our lawsuit, available here...    The documents also highlight the need for more transparency about safeguards against inappropriate, AI-driven denials. EFF has long argued that AI has no place in consequential government decisions about peoples' rights or access to benefits, such as immigration enforcement and policing decisions. That's because using automated decision-making in these contexts risks decisions that violate people's rights or deprive them of benefits they're entitled to based on biased or inappropriate considerations and without proper due process or accountability if there is an error.   By outsourcing decision-making to private AI companies without sufficient transparency, testing, or legal limits, WISeR jeopardizes seniors' access to medical care. Congress should step in to place greater legal limits on the use of automated decision-making in Medicare.  
The new documents "show why we need stronger legal limits around government use of automated decision-making..." according to the newsletter.  And another EFF page argues that the American public "still lacks the information needed to assess whether clinician review is providing meaningful oversight of AI systems and whether appropriate data is being used to evaluate prior authorization requests."
WISeR's payment structure gives vendors, as the government put it, "an incentive to deny as many claims as possible...."   [One company] denied more requests than it approved in the first few months of the program, and CMS inquired about "denials that appear inaccurate or inconsistent with applicable criteria."  Ultimately, the records obtained by EFF raise more questions than they answer about the safeguards used by WISeR vendors...
A growing body of scholarship points to the substantial limitations of "human in the loop" policies as guardrails for AI systems. AI-generated recommendations can unduly influence human decisions, leading reviewers to over-rely on automated judgements and rubber stamp them as correct. Even worse, at least one health insurance company actively pressured clinical reviewers to accept its AI systems' recommendations. Another company built a system that allowed clinical reviewers to reject claims without opening patient files; clinical reviewers using this system spent an average of just 1.2 seconds on each case.. 
As the government expands its use of automated decision-making, the potential for consequential mistakes increases rapidly. The records we've obtained so far raise questions about the rushed rollout and lack of guardrails for automated decision-making by the U.S. government. EFF urges transparency, oversight, and legal limits to protect people from the harms of automated decision-making in high risk systems.

articles.title: Everyone Always Wants Seconds of These Cheesy "Potato Puffs"
articles.body:
Cheesy “Potato Puffs” Are the Only Way I Eat Leftover Mashed Potatoes
Every Thanksgiving, if you’re lucky, you end up with just the right amount of leftovers for the perfectly stacked turkey sandwich or the loaded leftover lunch plate. But sometimes things get out of wack and you end up with way too much gravy or an extra casserole dish of stuffing. For me, the extra is often mashed potatoes, given my family’s propensity to go big on potatoes (my sister made over 10 pounds of potatoes this year!). But I don’t mind in the least, because these hot, cheesy little puffs are the perfect way to use up those mashed potatoes.
The Best Recipe to Use Up Mashed Potatoes
I first started making these a few years ago when left with an extra Dutch oven full of mashed potatoes and got tired of making mashed potato pancakes. I stirred up the potatoes with some eggs and a heaping helping of cheese, along with some bacon, and dolloped them into a mini muffin pan. (I especially love this pan, which has removable bottoms and is also so good for mini cheesecakes.)
Bake up and bam! Cheesy, tender little morsels of potatoes, with crisp edges and topped with sour cream or gravy (if you like!). They make a fantastic holiday weekend breakfast or appetizer. They are also a great way to use up little bits of leftovers from your holiday cooking: herbs, chopped turkey or ham, extra bacon.
It’s one of the few recipes where I actually like the leftover version better than the original. I eat them straight out of the pan;  just poke a spoon in and get at them. 
Get the recipe: Cheesy Mashed Potato Puffs
Do you have favorite ways of using up Thanksgiving leftovers?

articles.title: Kiri – The Modern Container Runtime
articles.body:
New0.2.1 Mac · Windows · Linux
The modern container runtime.
8× faster than Docker.
Kiri runs Docker containers with one daemon. The docker CLI, Compose and the Docker API work as they do today.
The 8×: docker run takes 22 ms on Kiri and 178 ms on Docker Desktop (152 ms on Colima, 279 ms on OrbStack), every engine on 2 CPUs and 8 GB.
Free, and in beta on Mac, Windows and Linux. Something broken or annoying? Tell us with Feedback in Kiri's window, and we fix it.
Kiri's window is now in 15 languages
- 简体中文
- 繁體中文
- 日本語
- 한국어
- Deutsch
- Français
- Español
- Italiano
- Português (Brasil)
- Polski
- Русский
- Türkçe
- Bahasa Indonesia
- Tiếng Việt
- English
Works with what
you already use
- docker
- docker compose
- docker buildx
- Docker Engine API
- Docker Hub
- OCI images
- ghcr.io
- Dockerfiles
While it runs
Light while it runs.
Ten containers running on one Apple silicon Mac, one runtime at a time: how much CPU and memory each one holds.
CPU and memory · 10 containers running
Sample One Apple-silicon Mac, one runtime at a time. Measured numbers replace these soon. Benchmarks →
What's in it
Everything you'd reach for Docker Desktop for.
Containers were the start. Kiri now builds and scans images, runs Kubernetes and whole Linux machines, and puts any container on the internet with one click.
- Containers and Compose Every docker command you use, Compose projects grouped in the window, and a page for each container with live logs, a shell and its files.
- Images from Docker Hub Search Docker Hub from the window and watch each layer pull. amd64 images run through Rosetta.
- Builds, with a scan docker build through BuildKit, a Builds view of every build, and a vulnerability scan of each image on its own page.
- Kubernetes kiri k8s start gives you a k3s cluster in about 20 seconds, with Pods and Services in the window. kind runs too.
- Linux machines kiri machine create dev --distro ubuntu: your user, sudo, and your Mac folders at the same paths.
- Share A public link for any container on runkiri.cloud, from the window or kiri share web. More.
- Names and HTTPS Apps open at web.kiri.local, Compose services at api.myapp.kiri.local, with HTTPS from Kiri's own narrow certificate authority.
- Light on your Mac Unused memory goes back while it runs, and the VM sleeps after a minute idle. The daemon stays around 15 MB; waking takes 0.15 s.
- Move over in one go Bring your images, volumes and containers from OrbStack or Docker Desktop, then switch docker to Kiri from the window.
Prefer the terminal?
The commands you already type.
With Kiri open, the ordinary docker command runs on Kiri, and kiri adds what Docker doesn't have: a name for every container, Kubernetes, Linux machines and a public link.
- kiri run, kiri ps work like their docker twins.
- web.kiri.localhost reaches a container by name, no port to remember.
- kiri k8s start and kiri machine create for a cluster or a Linux box.
- kiri share web puts it on the internet.
Getting started
From download to a public link in four steps.
- Step 1 Install Open the disk image and drag Kiri to Applications. It sets up docker for you.
Download for Mac
- Step 2 Pull an image Search Docker Hub in Images and press Pull, or: docker pull nginx
- Step 3 Run a container Press Run and give it a port. It starts in milliseconds. docker run -p 80:80 nginx
- Step 4 Share Press Share on the container for a public link, or: kiri share 80
Compare
Same command, three routes.
OrbStack and Docker Desktop pass every container start through five programs, each with its own socket. Kiri passes it through one daemon that calls the kernel itself. Same docker command on all three.
Five hops. One shim process stays resident for every running container.
The same five hops, and a shim per running container.
One daemon creates namespaces, cgroups and mounts itself. Nothing per container is left running. Most of this time is the docker CLI starting up. Through the Docker API, a whole container lifecycle takes 3.1 ms.
Medians from one full run on one Apple Silicon Mac, every engine limited to 2 CPUs and 8 GB, all three through the same docker CLI with Docker's default bridge networking. Stops are drawn evenly; only the totals are figures. Windows has its own race.
Full benchmarks: p99s, the Docker API path and every raw figure
How it works
One small VM. One daemon. A socket between them.
On macOS, Kiri boots a single Linux VM through Apple's Virtualization.framework, with a custom kernel and a small Rust init as PID 1. The host and guest talk over vsock. Inside, the Kiri daemon creates each container with clone3. On Linux the same daemon runs on your own kernel with no VM at all, and on Windows it runs inside WSL2.
One VM, one daemonSee the numbers
Boot once
One VM serves every container. Cold boot to ready takes 112 ms, down from 810 ms on a stock kernel.
Talk directly
Requests cross one vsock channel into the VM, not a chain of Unix sockets. A round trip takes 31 µs.
Leave nothing behind
No process stays per container. OrbStack keeps a shim for each one: 143 running containers held 1.13 GB in shims on our test Mac.
Measured on one Apple Silicon Mac. Method and raw numbers are on the benchmarks page.
The app
A native app, not a web wrapper.
AppKit and the system WebKit on the Mac, Win32 and WebView2 on Windows, so no Electron and no bundled browser. Manage containers, images, volumes, networks and Compose projects, with live stats, logs, a terminal and files for each container. Running apps open by name at myapp.kiri.local. On the Mac it brings your images and volumes over from OrbStack or Docker Desktop, and lives in the menu bar.
Download
Kiri for Mac is out.
Every number on this page was measured on it. Kiri sets up a kiri docker context and brings its own docker, Compose and buildx, so there's nothing else to install. Coming from OrbStack or Docker Desktop? Kiri brings your images and volumes over.
Then, in a new terminal:
$ docker run --rm hello-world
Same docker and docker compose you use today.

- Português (Brasil)

- Русский

- Bahasa Indonesia

- English
Works with what
you already use
- docker
- docker compose
- docker buildx
- Docker Engine API
- Docker Hub
- OCI images
- ghcr.io
- Dockerfiles
While it runs
Light while it runs.
Ten containers running on one Apple silicon Mac, one runtime at a time: how much CPU and memory each one holds.
CPU and memory · 10 containers running
Sample One Apple-silicon Mac, one runtime at a time. Measured numbers replace these soon. Benchmarks →
What's in it
Everything you'd reach for Docker Desktop for.
Containers were the start. Kiri now builds and scans images, runs Kubernetes and whole Linux machines, and puts any container on the internet with one click.
- Containers and Compose Every docker command you use, Compose projects grouped in the window, and a page for each container with live logs, a shell and its files.
- Images from Docker Hub Search Docker Hub from the window and watch each layer pull. amd64 images run through Rosetta.
- Builds, with a scan docker build through BuildKit, a Builds view of every build, and a vulnerability scan of each image on its own page.
- Kubernetes kiri k8s start gives you a k3s cluster in about 20 seconds, with Pods and Services in the window. kind runs too.
- Linux machines kiri machine create dev --distro ubuntu: your user, sudo, and your Mac folders at the same paths.
- Share A public link for any container on runkiri.cloud, from the window or kiri share web. More.
- Names and HTTPS Apps open at web.kiri.local, Compose services at api.myapp.kiri.local, with HTTPS from Kiri's own narrow certificate authority.
- Light on your Mac Unused memory goes back while it runs, and the VM sleeps after a minute idle. The daemon stays around 15 MB; waking takes 0.15 s.
- Move over in one go Bring your images, volumes and containers from OrbStack or Docker Desktop, then switch docker to Kiri from the window.
Prefer the terminal?
The commands you already type.
With Kiri open, the ordinary docker command runs on Kiri, and kiri adds what Docker doesn't have: a name for every container, Kubernetes, Linux machines and a public link.
- kiri run, kiri ps work like their docker twins.
- web.kiri.localhost reaches a container by name, no port to remember.
- kiri k8s start and kiri machine create for a cluster or a Linux box.
- kiri share web puts it on the internet.
Getting started
From download to a public link in four steps.
- Step 1 Install Open the disk image and drag Kiri to Applications. It sets up docker for you.
Download for Mac
- Step 2 Pull an image Search Docker Hub in Images and press Pull, or: docker pull nginx
- Step 3 Run a container Press Run and give it a port. It starts in milliseconds. docker run -p 80:80 nginx
- Step 4 Share Press Share on the container for a public link, or: kiri share 80
Compare
Same command, three routes.
OrbStack and Docker Desktop pass every container start through five programs, each with its own socket. Kiri passes it through one daemon that calls the kernel itself. Same docker command on all three.
Five hops. One shim process stays resident for every running container.
The same five hops, and a shim per running container.
One daemon creates namespaces, cgroups and mounts itself. Nothing per container is left running. Most of this time is the docker CLI starting up. Through the Docker API, a whole container lifecycle takes 3.1 ms.
Medians from one full run on one Apple Silicon Mac, every engine limited to 2 CPUs and 8 GB, all three through the same docker CLI with Docker's default bridge networking. Stops are drawn evenly; only the totals are figures. Windows has its own race.
Full benchmarks: p99s, the Docker API path and every raw figure
How it works
One small VM. One daemon. A socket between them.
On macOS, Kiri boots a single Linux VM through Apple's Virtualization.framework, with a custom kernel and a small Rust init as PID 1. The host and guest talk over vsock. Inside, the Kiri daemon creates each container with clone3. On Linux the same daemon runs on your own kernel with no VM at all, and on Windows it runs inside WSL2.
One VM, one daemonSee the numbers
Boot once
One VM serves every container. Cold boot to ready takes 112 ms, down from 810 ms on a stock kernel.
Talk directly
Requests cross one vsock channel into the VM, not a chain of Unix sockets. A round trip takes 31 µs.
Leave nothing behind
No process stays per container. OrbStack keeps a shim for each one: 143 running containers held 1.13 GB in shims on our test Mac.
Measured on one Apple Silicon Mac. Method and raw numbers are on the benchmarks page.
The app
A native app, not a web wrapper.
AppKit and the system WebKit on the Mac, Win32 and WebView2 on Windows, so no Electron and no bundled browser. Manage containers, images, volumes, networks and Compose projects, with live stats, logs, a terminal and files for each container. Running apps open by name at myapp.kiri.local. On the Mac it brings your images and volumes over from OrbStack or Docker Desktop, and lives in the menu bar.
Download
Kiri for Mac is out.
Every number on this page was measured on it. Kiri sets up a kiri docker context and brings its own docker, Compose and buildx, so there's nothing else to install. Coming from OrbStack or Docker Desktop? Kiri brings your images and volumes over.
Then, in a new terminal:
$ docker run --rm hello-world
Same docker and docker compose you use today.

articles.title: Osint Case Studies
articles.body:
These OSINT case studies start where the investigators finished. Every email address and alias in them was first printed by a court filing, a US Treasury sanctions entry or named investigative reporting, about a person who has been charged, convicted or sanctioned for cybercrime. In September 2026 we ran those identifiers through the OSINTsearch email lookup and username search, then wrote up what came back. This page indexes the series: what each post covers, the technique it teaches, and the lessons that hold across cases.
What these OSINT case studies are
Each post takes identifiers that are already public and asks two questions. How far does this address or alias travel on live platforms today? And what does that teach about investigation method? Six posts follow one case or group, from Scattered Spider to TeamPCP. Six are guides that draw on several cases to teach one technique. Together they work as OSINT investigation examples with every input shown.
Search results are presence and profile data layered on the record. A display name or location is whatever the account holder typed, and none of it replaces the record.
The method in plain language
- Start from a document that prints the identifier. An indictment, complaint, affidavit, sentencing memo, OFAC entry or named news report. Addresses that circulate online for well-known defendants but appear in no primary source are not searched.
- Copy it letter by letter. Krebs printed [email protected] in 2018 and [email protected] in 2019 for the same registration. One letter changes the result.
- Run each email through the email lookup. It checks about 175 platforms and reports registrations found, plus the profile where a platform exposes one: a GitHub handle, display name and creation date, for example.
- Run each alias through the username search. It checks about 760 platforms. Any handle the email side returned gets the same treatment.
- Put every date on the case timeline. Created before the alias existed, while it was in use, or after the name went public.
- Grade each result against the record, and log contradictions next to matches.
The case studies and guides
Khoroshev, Thomson, Coelho and Rudometov are charged, not convicted, and are presumed innocent, as is every other person here who has not been convicted.
Six lessons that hold across cases
Every example below comes from a post in the table.
1. The everyday mailbox is the one that talks
Persona addresses rarely identified anyone. The Fitzpatrick affidavit describes a Riseup address used to register on RaidForums; an email lookup found no registrations for it, consistent with that role, while the personal Gmail that Google records tie to him returned 11 registrations. In the TeamPCP case, the lookup found no registrations for the address the record ties to the BreachForums "Express" account, consistent with the forum-only use the record describes, while a Gmail Krebs tied to a Microsoft account in Thomson's name returned 24 results. Persona addresses were traced instead through what they touched, as the burner email post shows.
2. A coined handle is a fingerprint; a dictionary word is camouflage
volhvb returned 11 exact matches and no near misses. joeleoli returned 33 results, all exact matches. deadcatx3 returned 21 exact-match results, including the HackerOne profile Krebs reported. Common strings behave differently: Express, the BreachForums name Krebs ties to the group, returned 316 exact-match results and the TrickBot alias mango 439. A hit on a common word is a starting point, never an answer.
3. An email anchor beats a handle match
nerowolfe, the name of a fictional detective, returned 113 exact matches. Only one of them, the GitHub account reached through [email protected], is anchored to the public record, and it carries the NeroWolfe persona Krebs tied to Khoroshev. The same pattern holds for Grubbs, whose published Gmail resolves to a GitHub account displaying "Colton Grubbs", and for the OFAC address on Maksim Rudenskiy's entry, which resolves to a GitHub account displaying "Max Rudensky".
4. Dates sort owners from squatters
A creation date is the one profile field the owner cannot type. On the lockbitsupp alias, a Steam account held by an unrelated gamer dates from 2004, years before LockBit existed (Steam lets users change a profile URL, so the handle itself may be newer). A Codeforces account appeared five days after the indictment was unsealed and TikTok and Twitch accounts followed in December 2025, all possible squatters or impersonators. In the Joeleoli case, a GitLab profile displaying "Joel Evans" dates from September 2017, before the conspiracy he admitted, while a MyAnimeList account on the handle was created roughly 21 months after the arrest and carries the same squatter hedge. On the volhvb handle, none of the dated accounts was created after the designation.
5. The record anchors, and the search illustrates
The HackerOne profile at deadcatx3 displays "ruben thomson", exactly as Krebs reported. The Medium profile on volhvb displays the Cyrillic spelling of the name on the sanctions entry. Both mean something only because a public record had already tied the handle to the name. Good sources say so. Of his LockBit reconstruction, Krebs wrote: "Does the above timeline prove that NeroWolfe/Khoroshev is LockBitSupp? No." On a handle that appears nowhere in the record, a matching display name is a lead, not a conclusion.
6. Know which document prints identifiers
The Khoroshev indictment prints no email address at all, and the IntelBroker complaint refers to "West Email Account-1". The OFAC entry for Khoroshev prints two addresses. In the Scattered Spider cases, UK and European authorities published names, ages, towns and sentences but no alias, mailbox or handle; the US filings and journalists supplied the strings to search. Our SDN email guide shows how to find them on the list.
The ethics rules this series follows
- Public record only. Subjects are people publicly charged, convicted or sanctioned. Every identifier searched was first printed by a court, Treasury or named reporting, and every claim links to that source.
- Presumption of innocence. Charged means alleged. Persona ownership is attributed to whoever established it, such as "the NeroWolfe persona Krebs tied to him".
- No minors and no victims. Neither is identified or described.
- No unpublished handles. When a lookup surfaces a handle or display name the record never printed, the post describes it generically, for example as a profile whose display name matches the sanctioned name. Unrelated people who share a handle are never named.
- A zero result is not proof. A lookup that finds no registrations says what that lookup found, not that no account exists. A mailbox is called a persona or burner address only when the record describes it that way.
- Later accounts are hedged. Anything created after an arrest, unsealing or designation is treated as a possible squatter or impersonator.
- Some published details stay out. Phone numbers, passwords, passport and tax numbers, and relatives' details are left out even when a source prints them.
FAQ
What is an OSINT case study?
A worked example of open source investigation with its inputs shown: the identifier, the document that published it, the search run, and what came back. Here, every input is a public-record email or alias, so anyone can check the source and repeat the search.
Where do the identifiers in these case studies come from?
From indictments, complaints, affidavits, sentencing memos, OFAC sanctions entries and named reporting such as KrebsOnSecurity and BleepingComputer. The journalists and firms behind that work, including Intel 471 and OpenSanctions, deserve most of the credit.
Does a matching username or display name prove who owns an account?
No. A match shows a string is registered, and display names are self-typed. The attribution guide grades each kind of evidence, and the username verification checklist gives you a worksheet for the comparison.
Can I repeat these investigations myself?
Yes. Take an identifier from a primary source, run the email lookup first, search any handle it returns, sort the results by creation date and log results that contradict the record next to those that fit it.
Run your own case study
The method works on any lead, or on your own footprint. Run a free search on OSINTsearch for an email address or username. Results show the platform and profile details such as display names and join dates where available, and paid plans export to CSV, JSON or PDF.

articles.title: Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests
articles.body:
Diesem Problem waren wir alle ausgesetzt: Am Freitag gab es eine Störung, die den US-Softwarekonzern Microsoft lahmgelegt hat. Unter anderem das E-Mail-Programm Outlook.
Betroffen war auch das Phantasialand. Durch die Störung kamen keine Mails an, wie das Unternehmen dem WDR am Samstag mitteilte. So bekam niemand mit, dass das Wartungssicherheitssystem der Saunalandschaft längst per Mail Alarm geschlagen hat. Denn das automatischen Dosiersystem hatte zu viel Chlor in den Pool gepumpt.
Reizungen der Atemwege
Dadurch wurden Gäste im Hotel Ling Bao des Phantasialands in Brühl verletzt. Sie haben über gesundheitliche Probleme geklagt, nachdem sie den Pool besucht hatten. Der wurde zeitweise gesperrt, konnte inzwischen aber wieder freigegeben werden, wie die Feuerwehr am Samstag dem WDR mitteilte.
Wegen der Beschwerden der Hotel-Besucher wurden Rettungskräfte und die Feuerwehr gerufen. 13 Gäste klagten über Reizungen der Atemwege, letztlich stieg die Zahl der Betroffenen auf insgesamt 15.
Zunächst hieß es, dass fünf Gäste ins Krankenhaus gebracht wurden, später wurde die Zahl auf vier korrigiert, eine Person davon blieb wegen einer mittelschweren Verletzung zur Beobachtung im Krankenhaus.
Überhöhter Chlorgehalt
Im Hotel ergaben Tests der Einsatzkräfte einen Defekt des automatischen Dosiersystems für den Pool. Dies hatte zu einem deutlich überhöhten Chlorgehalt geführt. Das Wasser wurde daher ausgetauscht.
Unsere Quellen:
- Polizei Rhein-Erft-Kreis
- Feuerwehr Rhein-Erft-Kreis
- Pressemeldung Feuerwehr Brühl
- Birgit Reckersdrees, Direktion Marketing und Sales Phantasialand
Sendung: WDR2, WDR-Aktuell, 14.11.2026, 18 Uhr 
Sendung: WDR Fernsehen, WDR aktuell, 15.11.2026, 12.45 Uhr

articles.title: Huawei Set To Challenge Tesla Powerwall with New, 20 kW Home Battery
articles.body:
Huawei Set To Challenge Tesla Powerwall with New, 20 kW Home Battery (electrek.co) 13
			
		 	
				"Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery," reports Electrek:
This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla's latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark...  The Chinese tech firm is calling it an "all-in-one residential energy system" that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that's available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.  The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei's proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It's so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes. 
Huawei's basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with "just" 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That's enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you'll want to keep going if you're preparing for more than a day or two without power.  If that sounds like you, Luterra's got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can keep scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel. Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini).

articles.title: A NES emulator written in Odin
articles.body:
I made a NES emulator in Odin!
Intro
I’ve started this project in late June of 2024. I’ve worked on it in my spare time off and on. I decided to put a pause on this project in January 2025 to focus on other things.
I’ve learned so much about:
- The NES architecture, and possibly about game console architectures in general
- Bits and bytes, hex notation, and bitwise operations.
- The Odin programming language. I haven’t used it on a serious project before.
- How computers work. CPU instructions, “cycles”, etc
- Emulation. It’s very hard. Respect to emulator developers!
It’s been a wild ride. I’ve had a lot of fun, but I’ve also suffered more towards the end, when trying to make the emulator “fully” accurate.
You can read the Github Readme for more info about the project.
Features
- Enough emulation accuracy to run Battletoads and hundreds of other games perfectly.
- Debugger view with some debugging features
- Menu view to interact with the emulator
- Save states
- Controller support
- CRT Shader toggle
- (Partial) Sound
- Supported Mappers: NROM, MMC1, UXROM, CNROM, MMC3, GxROM, AxROM
Making an emulator
I’ve seen some people say that making a NES emulator is a simple weekend project, and I frankly found that baffling. Because evidently, it’s not. It took me 7 months to get my emulator to how it is now.
I think what they actually mean is that getting a NES emulator “working” takes a short time. Like maybe getting Donkey Kong to run. And that’s true. You can get to 80% or maybe 90% pretty fast. It’s the last 10% that takes a long, long time.
The NES hardware has many idiosyncrasies that need to be emulated for certain games to run. Many games depend on very specific NES behavior. And if you don’t implement it right, they won’t run. A lot of the challenge is about timing. The CPU and the PPU (the chip that handles the graphics rendering in the NES) run in parallel and they communicate with each other. That timing needs to be very accurate, or many wrong things can happen. Most games will run fine with a less than accurate emulator, but a lot of them won’t, and they will need you to consider things in more detail.
Another issue is mappers. Mappers are what we call an implementation of a type of cartridge. You see, NES games come in cartridges, and cartridges aren’t just data. They are circuitry with their own behavior and extra resources like read-only memory, and writable memory. Some come with extra audio capabilities, but I haven’t implemented that.
Anyway, you have to implement these mappers if you want a game that comes in that cartridge to run in your game. They complete the NES’s circuitry. In a way, they are a part of the NES hardware. There are many mappers, but you can support a lot of games by just implementing a few. I’ve had trouble implementing some mappers, and some of them are still badly implemented, causing some games to not work. I found it hard to understand some of the mapper documentation.
The biggest challenge with making an emulator, I think, is to know what to implement. Information about the hardware, and what needs to be emulated about the hardware for games to work in your emulator. Thankfully, the NES is very well documented online. I’ve used many resources, like:
- The Nesdev wiki
- The nesdev wiki discord. People here have helped me with my issues a lot.
- Javidx’s NES series. The code has many mistakes but it’s a good starting point.
- This article about the NES’s PPU
- Test ROMS. These NES ROMS thoroughly test particular aspects of your emulator. This is an extraordinary tool to accelerate development of emulator accuracy.
I wouldn’t have been able to do any of this without these resources and the help from people in the nesdev discord.
Odin
I’ve learned a lot about Odin while making this project. I think it fit this project like a glove. Being a very simple, strongly typed C-like language that gives me all the freedom I want makes making an emulator much easier than using other languages, I feel.
One thing that threw me off was that Odin has no automatic integer promotion. When doing calculations on numbers, Odin will never promote types to a bigger one. That led to a few bugs. But I blame this all on me and me being used to C’s integer promotion.
One fun thing that I’ve learned was doing a bit of memory allocation strategy. Odin has no automatic memory management, so you have to come up with smart ways to handle memory. I’ve had fun thinking about how I should handle memory best. I didn’t need to do anything complicated. I mostly use one temporary allocator that clears every frame, a global heap allocator for things that need to live forever, and a NES Arena allocator for anything that needs to live along a NES session. I found memory allocation fun.
Another thing I had to learn is how to serialize Odin objects. I used the CBOR library, and I ran into a few issues. I thought my code was misbehaving due to a bug in the library, but that was cleared up. It was only having trouble because I made a few odd types that it didn’t know how to serialize. Once I learned how to properly write custom handling for types, everything worked perfectly. This was one of the tricky types that cbor didn’t know how to serialize:
PpuCtrl :: struct #raw_union {
	// VPHB SINN
	using flags: bit_field u8 {
		n: u8 | 2,
		i: u8 | 1,
		s: u8 | 1, // sprite pattern table address for 8x8 sprites (0: $0000, 1: $1000)
		b: u8 | 1, // bg pattern table address (0: $0000, 1: $1000)
		h: u8 | 1, // sprite size (0: 8x8, 1: 8x16)
		p: u8 | 1,
		v: u8 | 1, // vblank NMI enable
	},
	reg:         u8,
}
I love how Odin lets you define raw unions like this, and with bit fields. It fits emulator development very well.
What’s missing
I don’t consider this project “finished”. Of course, a project like this is never truly finished, but a lot of aspects of it need a lot of work, for sure:
- The sound. lucyNES doesn’t sound very well still. Some games will sound fine but most won’t. I have to improve the implementation, and implement the DMC channel which I haven’t done.
- Some games that I’ve tested don’t work due to a poor mapper implementation
- I could implement more mappers so more games are supported.
These are the main things that are lacking at this moment. Maybe at some point I will return and keep working on this so the project can feel “complete”.

Another thing I had to learn is how to serialize Odin objects. I used the CBOR library, and I ran into a few issues. I thought my code was misbehaving due to a bug in the library, but that was cleared up. It was only having trouble because I made a few odd types that it didn’t know how to serialize. Once I learned how to properly write custom handling for types, everything worked perfectly. This was one of the tricky types that cbor didn’t know how to serialize:
PpuCtrl :: struct #raw_union {
	// VPHB SINN
	using flags: bit_field u8 {
		n: u8 | 2,
		i: u8 | 1,
		s: u8 | 1, // sprite pattern table address for 8x8 sprites (0: $0000, 1: $1000)
		b: u8 | 1, // bg pattern table address (0: $0000, 1: $1000)
		h: u8 | 1, // sprite size (0: 8x8, 1: 8x16)
		p: u8 | 1,
		v: u8 | 1, // vblank NMI enable
	},
	reg:         u8,
}
I love how Odin lets you define raw unions like this, and with bit fields. It fits emulator development very well.
What’s missing
I don’t consider this project “finished”. Of course, a project like this is never truly finished, but a lot of aspects of it need a lot of work, for sure:
- The sound. lucyNES doesn’t sound very well still. Some games will sound fine but most won’t. I have to improve the implementation, and implement the DMC channel which I haven’t done.
- Some games that I’ve tested don’t work due to a poor mapper implementation
- I could implement more mappers so more games are supported.
These are the main things that are lacking at this moment. Maybe at some point I will return and keep working on this so the project can feel “complete”.

articles.title: Eclipse Mosquitto – An open source MQTT broker
articles.body:
Mosquitto is an open source implementation of a server for version 5.0, 3.1.1,
and 3.1 of the MQTT protocol. It also includes a C and C++ client library,
the mosquitto_pub mosquitto_rr, and mosquitto_sub utilities for
publishing and subscribing, and the mosquitto_ctrl, mosquitto_signal, and
mosquitto_passwd applications for helping administer the broker.
See the following links for more information on MQTT:
- Community page: http://mqtt.org/
- MQTT v3.1.1 standard: https://docs.oasis-open.org/mqtt/mqtt/v3.1.1/mqtt-v3.1.1.html
- MQTT v5.0 standard: https://docs.oasis-open.org/mqtt/mqtt/v5.0/mqtt-v5.0.html
Mosquitto project information is available at the following locations:
- Main homepage: https://mosquitto.org/
- Find existing bugs or submit a new bug: https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto/issues
- Source code repository: https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto
There is also a public test server available at https://test.mosquitto.org/
See https://mosquitto.org/download/ for details on installing binaries for various platforms.
If you have installed a binary package the broker should have been started automatically. If not, it can be started with a very basic configuration:
mosquitto
Then use mosquitto_sub to subscribe to a topic:
mosquitto_sub -t 'test/topic' -v
And to publish a message:
mosquitto_pub -t 'test/topic' -m 'hello world'
Note that starting the broker like this allows anonymous/unauthenticated access but only from the local computer, so it's only really useful for initial testing.
If you want to have clients from another computer connect, you will need to
provide a configuration file. If you have installed from a binary package, you
will probably already have a configuration file at somewhere like
/etc/mosquitto/mosquitto.conf. If you've compiled from source, you can write
your config file then run as mosquitto -c /path/to/mosquitto.conf.
To start your config file you define a listener and you will need to think about what authentication you require. It is not advised to run your broker with anonymous access when it is publicly available.
For details on how to do this, look at the authentication methods available and the dynamic security plugin.
Documentation for the broker, clients and client library API can be found in
the man pages, which are available online at https://mosquitto.org/man/. There
are also pages with an introduction to the features of MQTT, the
mosquitto_passwd utility for dealing with username/passwords, and a
description of the configuration file options available for the broker.
Detailed client library API documentation can be found at https://mosquitto.org/api/
To build from source the recommended route for end users is to download the archive from https://mosquitto.org/download/.
On Windows and Mac, use cmake to build. On other platforms, just run make
to build. For Windows, see also README-windows.md.
If you are building from the git repository then the documentation will not
already be built. Use make binary to skip building the man pages, or install
docbook-xsl on Debian/Ubuntu systems.
- cJSON - required
- c-ares (libc-ares-dev on Debian based systems) - optional, enable with
WITH_SRV=yes
- libedit - for mosquitto_ctrl interactive shell - optional, disable with
WITH_EDITLINE=no
- libmicrohttpd - for broker http api support - optional, disable with
WITH_HTTP_API=no
- openssl (libssl-dev on Debian based systems) - optional, disable with
WITH_TLS=no
- pthreads - for client library thread support. This is required to support the
mosquitto_loop_start() and mosquitto_loop_stop() functions. If compiled
without pthread support, the library isn't guaranteed to be thread safe.
- sqlite3 - for persistence support in the broker - optional, disable with
WITH_SQLITE=no
- uthash / utlist - bundled versions of these headers are provided, disable
their use with WITH_BUNDLED_DEPS=no
- xsltproc (xsltproc and docbook-xsl on Debian based systems) - only needed
when building from git sources - disable with WITH_DOCS=no
Equivalent options for enabling/disabling features are available when using the CMake build. It is also possible to enable/disable building of specific plugins in the CMake build.
You can download and install mosquitto using the vcpkg dependency manager:
git clone https://github.com/Microsoft/vcpkg.git
cd vcpkg
./bootstrap-vcpkg.sh
./vcpkg integrate install
./vcpkg install mosquitto
The mosquitto port in vcpkg is kept up to date by Microsoft team members and community contributors. If the version is out of date, please create an issue or pull request on the vcpkg repository.
Mosquitto was written by Roger Light roger@atchoo.org. There have been substantial contributions by other people in the community both in terms of code and other help.
